editions.headline: Today's Healthcare Insights
editions.subheadline: A cross-source executive briefing on healthcare policy, operations, and market signals.
editions.summary_note: CMS proposed a 2028 Medicare Advantage rule that would cut Star Ratings to 15 measures, along with ADVaNCE MA, a mandatory model replacing stars with state-based Diamond Ratings in select states. Kaufman Hall data show the median hospital margin fell to 1.1%, with nearly half of hospitals losing money, while Oracle defended a $17 billion VA EHR cost increase and the FDA rejected Capricor's Duchenne therapy over data-integrity concerns. Sources include CMS, STAT, Healthcare Dive, BioPharma Dive, MedTech Dive, MedCity News, KFF Health News, Fierce Pharma and Becker's.

editorial_buckets.name: Policy, Payment, and Regulation
editorial_buckets.synthesis: CMS released its second 2028 Medicare Advantage and Part D proposed rule, which would cut Star Ratings to 15 measures, move network-adequacy proof to a plan's first operating year and set a whole-food standard for food benefits. Alongside it, CMMI proposed ADVaNCE MA, a mandatory model that would replace Star Ratings with state-based Diamond Ratings in select states starting in 2029. HHS also funded $47 million in MAHA ELEVATE lifestyle pilots in Medicare. On the Hill, Democrats pressed Oz on delayed rural transformation awards, consumer groups pushed for patent reform before year-end, and KFF analysis shows Medicare for All support depends heavily on how it is framed.

items.title: CMS's 2028 Medicare Advantage rule would cut Star Ratings to 15 measures, delay network-adequacy proof and set a 'healthy food' standard
items.summary: CMS's second proposed rule for contract year 2028 (CMS-4214-P2), issued Nov. 20, would focus MA and Part D Star Ratings on 15 measures weighted toward outcomes and patient experience, raise the bar for high ratings and bonus payments, and remove the reward factor. New plans would demonstrate network adequacy in their first operating year instead of at application, and three behavioral health specialty types would merge into one for network counts. Food and beverage supplemental benefits would have to meet a whole-food standard tied to the 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines. Other provisions cap emergency cost sharing at $180-$240, require plans to keep in-network rates for at least 90 days after a significant provider termination, and route prior-authorization requests through FHIR-based APIs.
items.strategic_implication: This is the rule that sets 2028 bids, and the Star Ratings changes reach the 2030 ratings that drive bonus dollars. Plans should model which of their current strong measures fall away. Providers gain leverage from the 90-day continuity protection and the FHIR prior-auth requirement, and should check whether their contracting and interface roadmaps match. Comments are due 60 days after Federal Register publication.

items.title: CMMI proposes ADVaNCE MA, a mandatory 10-year model that would replace Star Ratings with state-based 'Diamond Ratings' in select states
items.summary: Alongside the 2028 rule, the CMS Innovation Center proposed ADVaNCE MA, a mandatory 10-year model starting Jan. 1, 2029, after a pre-implementation period that begins June 8, 2027. In the selected states, which CMS would name in the final 2028 rule, Diamond Ratings would replace Star Ratings and Quality Bonus Payments, comparing plans against others in the same state with similar populations. HMOs, local PPOs, PFFS plans, C-SNPs and D-SNPs would participate; state Medicaid directors could opt out their D-SNPs. The model would also let plans target food, transportation and caregiver benefits to Part D Low-Income Subsidy enrollees and would shadow-test an 'inferred' risk adjustment model that would not be used for payment.
items.strategic_implication: A mandatory model that swaps the national quality bonus system for state-by-state comparisons would reshuffle which plans win bonus money, and national carriers would face different scoring rules in different states. The shadow risk-adjustment test is an early sign of where CMS wants to take coding-driven payment. Plans and provider-sponsored plans should comment on how states will be selected and how the model will interact with existing star-ratings litigation.

items.title: HHS funds $47 million MAHA ELEVATE pilots to test whether 'food is medicine' and lifestyle programs should be covered by Medicare
items.summary: HHS announced MAHA ELEVATE, a Medicare pilot in which 15 groups will test nutrition, exercise and other lifestyle programs, such as cooking classes and nutrition coaching for people with chronic conditions, for effects on beneficiaries' health and federal spending. STAT reports $47 million in funding. CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz said the goal is to 'make it easier to be healthy in America.' Medicare does not cover many of these interventions today, and the pilots are meant to generate evidence over several years on whether coverage is warranted. Full award details sit behind STAT's paywall.
items.strategic_implication: Together with the MA healthy-food standard, this shows CMS building the evidence base for nutrition benefits in both traditional Medicare and MA. Health systems and community organizations running food-is-medicine programs should track the 15 awardees and their measures, since those outcomes are likely to shape future coverage and MA benefit design.

items.title: 18 congressional Democrats demand answers from Oz on the delayed second-year Rural Health Transformation awards
items.summary: Eighteen congressional Democrats wrote to CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz seeking answers on the nine-day delay in second-year awards from the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, citing 'an alarming lack of public transparency.' Awards were due Oct. 31; CMS cited 'an additional administrative process requirement' and announced them Nov. 9. Most state awards changed less than 2% from year one; North Dakota and Iowa gained the most, while New Jersey, Florida and Vermont saw the largest reductions. The lawmakers asked for a searchable spending database, a performance evaluation plan and a briefing, with answers due Nov. 25. Five rural hospitals have closed or converted since the fund was created.
items.strategic_implication: With Democrats taking both chambers in January, RHTP oversight is likely to turn into formal hearings and data requests. States and rural providers should expect more scrutiny of how year-one money was spent and should document results now. Florida's reduced award matters for in-state rural planning.

items.title: 15 consumer groups push Congress to pass patent-thicket and pay-for-delay bills before year-end
items.summary: Fifteen consumer advocacy groups led by Families USA urged Congress to reform drug patent law before the end of the year, targeting patent thickets, 'product hopping' and pay-for-delay settlements. They named the ETHIC Act, the Affordable Prescriptions for Patients Act and the Preserve Access to Affordable Generics and Biosimilars Act. The letter points to Amgen's challenge of Colorado's upper payment limit on Enbrel, whose list price has risen more than 1,500% since 1998, and warns that a win could make federal patents 'a shield against every state affordability standard.' At least 11 states have prescription drug affordability boards, and four have upper payment limit authority.
items.strategic_implication: The Amgen-Colorado case is the one to watch: if patents can preempt state upper payment limits, the state PDAB route to drug cost control narrows sharply. Patent bills have stalled for two years, as last week's Senate Judiciary hearing showed, so health systems and employers should plan on drug-cost relief coming, if at all, from the next Congress.

items.title: Medicare for All is back in play, but KFF polling shows support swings from three-quarters to the 20s depending on framing
items.summary: Julie Rovner writes that Democrats, who won House and Senate majorities, now have to choose between restoring Trump-era cuts to Medicaid and ACA subsidies and pursuing broader coverage expansion. Candidates backing universal coverage won Senate seats in Michigan, Maine, Iowa and Texas, and presumptive Speaker Hakeem Jeffries supports lowering the Medicare eligibility age and covering all children. KFF's September poll found Medicare for All support at its highest level since regular tracking began, but KFF's Mollyann Brodie says support can reach three-quarters when framed as guaranteed care and fall to the 20s when framed around taxes. Any bill faces a likely veto, and Medicare's hospital trust fund is projected to run out in 2033.
items.strategic_implication: Expect 2027 to bring messaging bills and hearings rather than law. The near-term policy fight is over restoring ACA subsidies and Medicaid funding, while Medicare-at-55 and coverage for children are the incremental options most likely to be scored and debated. Systems and plans should prepare positions on those narrower proposals.

editorial_buckets.name: Digital Health and AI
editorial_buckets.synthesis: Oracle's CEO defended a $17 billion increase to the VA EHR contract ceiling before House lawmakers. KFF Health News reports patients suing over sensor-equipped knee implants they say they never agreed to, as Medicare remote-monitoring spending passed $500 million. HLTH takeaways point to agentic AI in prior auth and scheduling, and a STAT essay warns that an AI market downturn could strand hospitals before they finish evaluating their tools.

items.title: Oracle CEO defends a $17 billion increase to the VA EHR contract ceiling as House Democrats call it a 'blank check'
items.summary: Oracle CEO Mike Sicilia told the House Veterans' Affairs Committee that a $17 billion increase in the VA EHR contract ceiling, to $27 billion, is 'an estimate to finish the deployments' and 'not a commitment to spend at Oracle.' He said task orders would be fixed-price, with Oracle absorbing overruns, and that the intended user base grew 129%, from 85,000 in 2022 to 195,000. Ranking member Mark Takano said he saw no justification for the increase. The VA paused the program in 2023 with 5 of 170 medical centers live, restarted in April 2026 with 13 sites, plans 26 more next year and targets all 170 by 2031. Senators questioned Sicilia the day before.
items.strategic_implication: For VA-adjacent providers and community care partners, the 2027 wave of 26 sites is the operational milestone to plan around. For other health systems, the hearing is a reminder of how far scope and training costs can push EHR budgets past initial estimates. Incoming Democratic control of the committees in January points to tighter oversight of the spending ceiling.

items.title: Patients sue over 'smart' knee implants they say they never agreed to, as Medicare remote-monitoring spending passes $500 million
items.summary: Two patients are suing Zimmer Biomet, Canary Medical and their surgeons, alleging they received Persona IQ sensor-equipped knee implants without informed consent; one says the device later kept him from getting an MRI. Zimmer's own website says the implant is 'not intended to support clinical decision-making' and 'has not been shown to provide any clinical benefit,' though the company says nearly 90% of surveyed recipients would choose it again. Nearly 1 million Medicare beneficiaries received remote patient monitoring in 2024, and Medicare paid $536 million for it, more than double the amount three years earlier. HHS's inspector general found 43% of those patients did not receive all required components of the service.
items.strategic_implication: Remote monitoring billing is growing faster than the evidence behind it, and the OIG is watching. Orthopedic programs that use connected implants should review consent forms, MRI-compatibility disclosures and RPM billing documentation. Payers may tighten RPM coverage criteria for devices without demonstrated clinical benefit.

items.title: HLTH wrap-up: agentic AI moves into prior auth and scheduling, while affordability and GLP-1 costs dominate payer talk
items.summary: Healthcare Dive's HLTH 2026 takeaways note that OpenAI announced partnerships on computer-use agents for insurance preapprovals and discharge planning, and AWS rolled out patient-facing Amazon Health Connect tools for booking, identity verification and prescriptions. AWS said UC San Diego cut staff phone time by 630 hours a week and abandoned calls by about 30%. Morgan Health's Dan Mendelson said GLP-1 coverage can reach 5% of employers' total medical spending, and Twin Health said two-thirds of patients stop within a year. Coalition for Health AI CEO Brian Anderson warned that digital tools have historically widened both the digital divide and costs.
items.strategic_implication: The practical AI story out of HLTH is front-office and utilization-management automation with measurable labor savings, not clinical decision-making. Access centers and revenue cycle teams should benchmark vendor claims against the UC San Diego figures. Employers remain the pressure point on GLP-1 spending.

items.title: Opinion: if the AI investment bubble bursts, hospitals could lose tools before they finish proving whether they work
items.summary: In a STAT First Opinion essay, pathologist-researcher David Adler argues that an AI market downturn, following the Oct. 30 sell-off that Anthropic's Nov. 19 IPO did not reverse, could leave hospitals without vendors before evaluations are complete. He cites cancer-trial matching studies at Penn and Emory and in Australia in which AI improved eligibility accuracy or found more eligible patients but did not increase enrollment. 'A health AI company's market value and the medical value of its technology are two different things,' he writes. He recommends that hospitals set clear success criteria up front and keep research data so tools can be evaluated independently if a vendor scales back or closes.
items.strategic_implication: This is an opinion piece, but the risk is concrete for systems with many early-stage AI vendors. AI governance committees should add vendor financial health, data portability and exit terms to contracting checklists, and should define outcome measures before deployment rather than after.

editorial_buckets.name: Market and Industry Signals
editorial_buckets.synthesis: Sanofi is weighing a bid for Insmed, valued above $30 billion, to offset its Dupixent patent cliff. The FDA rejected Capricor's Duchenne therapy a second time and publicly cited data-integrity violations, while approving Beren's Lembaz for Niemann-Pick type C on survival data. Compass and Usona are racing for the first psilocybin approval, and Zimmer filed for clearance of an autonomous knee robot.

items.title: Sanofi weighs a takeover of Insmed, valued above $30 billion, to offset its Dupixent patent cliff
items.summary: Bloomberg reported that Sanofi is working with advisers on a possible acquisition of Insmed, whose bronchiectasis drug Brinsupri was the first DPP1 inhibitor on the U.S. market. Insmed reported more than $917 million in Brinsupri sales in the first nine months of 2026 and guided to $1.35 billion to $1.4 billion for the year; Mizuho projects $6.6 billion in peak sales. Insmed's market value reached $31 billion at the Nov. 20 close, up 18% in two days. Analysts say a price near $40 billion would test Sanofi's balance sheet, which carries about EUR 12 billion in net debt. Talks could take weeks and may not produce a deal.
items.strategic_implication: A deal of this size would be one of the year's largest and would signal how far big pharma will pay for de-risked, launched assets ahead of patent cliffs. Respiratory and pulmonary programs should expect stronger commercial support behind Brinsupri either way, and pharmacy teams should watch for pricing and contracting changes if ownership changes.

items.title: FDA rejects Capricor's Duchenne cell therapy a second time and accuses the company of 'serious data integrity violations'
items.summary: The FDA again turned down deramiocel, Capricor's donor-derived cardiac cell therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, saying the data were not 'sufficient to establish substantial evidence of effectiveness.' In an unusual public statement, the agency also cited 'serious data integrity violations,' including breaches of study blinding and after-the-fact changes to the statistical analysis plan. Capricor said HOPE-3 met both main goals and CEO Linda Marban said the company stands behind its data. The FDA first rejected the therapy in July 2025. More than two dozen investigators supported approval, but an advisory committee majority found no clear evidence of benefit.
items.strategic_implication: The FDA is making its reasoning public in high-profile rare-disease decisions, as it did with Summit's ivonescimab letter last week. For sponsors, protecting the blind and locking analysis plans before unblinding are now reputational risks, not just regulatory ones. Duchenne families and treating centers lose a near-term option.

items.title: FDA approves Beren's Lembaz, the first Niemann-Pick type C therapy with a survival benefit, after a 20-year development path
items.summary: The FDA approved Beren Therapeutics' Lembaz (adrabetadex) on Nov. 17 to reduce the risk of death in children and adults with Niemann-Pick disease type C whose neurological symptoms began before age 6. Beren reported median survival of 8.5 years in treated patients versus 4.9 years in an external control. The molecule began with NIH natural-history research in 2006 and passed through Vtesse, Sucampo and Mallinckrodt, which abandoned it after a failed trial and its 2020 bankruptcy, before Beren bought it in 2021. Hearing loss carries a boxed warning. Beren plans an early-December launch, has not disclosed a price and received a rare pediatric disease priority review voucher.
items.strategic_implication: This is a case study in rescuing an abandoned asset with NIH-generated natural-history data and external controls, a path the FDA is increasingly accepting in ultra-rare disease. Pediatric specialty pharmacies and payers should prepare for another high-cost orphan therapy alongside Miplyffa and Aqneursa, with audiology monitoring built into the care pathway.

items.title: Compass and Usona race for the first psilocybin approval, with an estimated $34,000-a-year price and in-clinic dosing shaping access
items.summary: Compass Pathways has filed COMP360 for treatment-resistant depression, and an analyst reports that Usona Institute has filed PSIL201 for major depressive disorder using an FDA national priority voucher; Usona has not confirmed its filing or released Phase 3 data. Citeline estimates COMP360's list price at about $34,000 a year based on two to four doses, and RBC projects $1.9 billion in peak sales in treatment-resistant depression alone. Stifel analysts question whether Usona's six-week blinded period will satisfy FDA and noted that CDER head Michael Davis previously worked at Usona. Each dose requires several hours in clinic with trained staff.
items.strategic_implication: The real limit on psilocybin uptake will be care delivery: dosing rooms, monitoring staff, and step therapy requirements for patients who fail generics first. Behavioral health service lines should start sizing space and staffing models now, and payers will likely require prior treatment failures, as they do for Spravato.

items.title: Zimmer files for FDA clearance of an autonomous knee-replacement robot, aiming for a 2027 launch a year ahead of plan
items.summary: Zimmer Biomet submitted a 510(k) for a fully autonomous version of the Monogram orthopedic robot it acquired for $177 million in 2025, and hopes for clearance in 2027 rather than the 2028 timeline it originally set. Unlike its existing Rosa robot, Monogram works with CT imaging. CEO Ivan Tornos said the trial had no safety events and called it a 'game-changing platform,' but added, 'I wouldn't be surprised if there's some back and forth with the FDA, given that this is new-to-the-world technology.' Surgeons at a Stifel conference said it could save time, reduce instrument trays and ease physical strain.
items.strategic_implication: An autonomous cutting robot would test FDA's framework and hospitals' credentialing and liability policies. Orthopedic service lines planning capital purchases for 2027 should factor in this option and the separate scrutiny Zimmer faces over its sensor-equipped Persona IQ knee.

editorial_buckets.name: Provider Operations
editorial_buckets.synthesis: Kaufman Hall data show the median hospital operating margin fell to 1.1% through September, with nearly half of hospitals losing money and uncompensated care rising ahead of 2027 Medicaid changes. J&J will place its first U.S. Ottava robot at Memorial Hermann, giving buyers two major alternatives to Intuitive in general surgery. In Iowa, two rival critical access hospitals are jointly building a foundation-funded cancer center.

items.title: Kaufman Hall: median hospital operating margin falls to 1.1% and nearly half of hospitals are losing money
items.summary: Kaufman Hall's latest data from more than 1,300 hospitals put the median year-to-date operating margin through September at 1.1%, down from more than 3% through the summer, with nearly half of hospitals and health systems operating at a loss. Bad debt and charity care as a share of gross operating revenue rose 8% from a year earlier and 13% from three years earlier. Daily net operating revenue rose 6%, and outpatient revenue is up nearly a third over three years. Managing director Erik Swanson said providers are vulnerable to even slight revenue reductions as states prepare Medicaid work requirements for the first half of 2027, which research suggests could remove up to 10.1 million people from Medicaid.
items.strategic_implication: Margins this thin leave little room before the 2027 coverage losses hit. CFOs should stress-test 2027 budgets for higher uncompensated care, accelerate financial-assistance screening and Medicaid enrollment help, and check bond covenant headroom. Swanson's 'double-edged sword' warning on outpatient growth suggests reviewing whether new ambulatory capacity is pulling volume from inpatient settings that carry fixed costs.

items.title: Memorial Hermann-Texas Medical Center will be the first U.S. hospital to install J&J's Ottava surgical robot
items.summary: Johnson & Johnson said Memorial Hermann-Texas Medical Center in Houston will be the first U.S. hospital to commercially install and use its Ottava robotic surgery system through an early-access program. The FDA granted Ottava de novo authorization in July 2026 for 10 upper-abdominal procedures, including gastric bypass, cholecystectomy, appendectomy and hernia repair. Its four arms are built into a standard surgical table to save operating-room space. The same week, Medtronic said its Hugo robot won expanded FDA clearance for upper-abdominal general surgery, so Intuitive now faces two major competitors in general surgery.
items.strategic_implication: With three major vendors now cleared in general surgery, health systems have more leverage on robot pricing, service contracts and placement terms than they did when Intuitive was effectively the only option. Perioperative leaders planning 2027 capital should seek competing bids and assess OR footprint and training requirements.

items.title: Two competing Iowa critical access hospitals build a $14.3 million shared cancer center to bring radiation therapy home
items.summary: Pella Regional Health Center and Knoxville Hospital & Clinics, independent critical access hospitals about 15 miles apart in Marion County, Iowa, formed a joint venture to build a 7,800-square-foot cancer center with a linear accelerator and PET/CT scanner. The $14.3 million project is funded entirely through a capital campaign run by the hospitals' foundations and is scheduled to open in February 2027. It is the first time the two hospitals have partnered on radiation therapy. Knoxville's CEO said roughly half of its cancer patients need radiation and families had asked why it was not available locally.
items.strategic_implication: Competitor joint ventures are a practical model for rural service lines that neither hospital could support alone, and foundation-funded capital avoids adding debt. Rural leaders, and states deploying Rural Health Transformation funds, should look at shared specialty services like this as an alternative to full mergers.

editorial_buckets.name: Workforce & Clinical Practice
editorial_buckets.synthesis: The USPSTF met for the first time since March 2025 but voted privately, while AHRQ's director removed subpopulation data from recommendations. Turmoil at the American Diabetes Association raises questions about its December standards of care. UMMS is offering its nurse orientation tool to other systems after avoiding about $4 million in labor costs, and the ICE detention of a Princeton researcher adds to concerns about international research talent.

items.title: At its first meeting since March 2025, USPSTF votes in private as AHRQ's director strips subpopulation data from recommendations
items.summary: The 16-member U.S. Preventive Services Task Force voted on recommendations for cervical cancer screening, perinatal depression and unhealthy alcohol use, but cast its votes privately even though the meeting was livestreamed. STAT reports that AHRQ director Roger Klein removed subpopulation data from recommendation language under an administration policy requiring removal of DEI language. Member Alicia Fernandez warned that edits by political leadership could undermine perceptions of the panel's scientific independence. Members also raised concerns about bias among expert presenters and about documenting AI use in evidence reviews.
items.strategic_implication: Task Force 'A' and 'B' grades drive ACA no-cost coverage, so any perceived politicization creates both clinical and coverage uncertainty. Quality and population health teams should note the removal of subpopulation data, which affects how targeted screening outreach is justified, and watch for the published cervical cancer and perinatal depression recommendations.

items.title: American Diabetes Association turmoil raises questions about its December standards of care and journal independence
items.summary: The American Diabetes Association is facing a 1,221-member boycott, resignations and dismissals after five members were removed by armed security from its June meeting for distributing an editorial critical of NIH funding cuts before NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya spoke. Diabetes Care editor-in-chief Steven Kahn and deputy editors joined the boycott, and publications vice president Chris Kohler resigned Nov. 6, citing threats to editorial independence. The ADA has appointed interim journal editors and says it will publish their names. Its 2027 standards of care are due in December and were nearly complete, while the agenda for the June 2027 meeting is not set.
items.strategic_implication: The ADA standards of care underpin diabetes quality measures, formularies and payer policies. Clinical leaders should review the December release closely, and quality teams should watch whether any changes appear without the usual journal and expert review.

items.title: University of Maryland Medical System offers its nurse orientation tool to other systems after avoiding about $4 million in labor costs
items.summary: UMMS is making its nurse-designed Orientation Assessment Reporting System (OARS) available to other health systems through its iHarbor innovation studio. The tool tracks new nurses' readiness for independent practice and gives preceptors and managers standardized progress data. From January 2023 through Nov. 4, 2026, UMMS links it to a net reduction of 3,439 orientation shifts, about $4 million in avoided labor costs, across 125 units and 2,205 orientees. Developer Susie Williams said the tool 'isn't intended to rush nurses through orientation' and also flags nurses who need more support. Its effect on retention has not been measured.
items.strategic_implication: Orientation length is a large and rarely measured nursing cost. CNOs can use standardized readiness data to shorten orientation for nurses who are ready and extend it for those who are not. Systems weighing OARS or similar tools should require retention and safety outcomes, not just shift savings.

items.title: ICE detention of a Princeton neuroscience PhD student after a conference deepens worries about international research talent
items.summary: ICE detained Eva Yi Xie, a third-year Princeton PhD student working in neuroscience and AI who has lived in the U.S. since 2016, as she traveled home from the Society for Neuroscience meeting in Washington. The New York Times reported her visa had expired; her lawyers said she has a pending asylum application and is legally allowed to remain. Princeton's graduate dean called the news 'distressing' and said the university arranged legal representation. STAT notes smaller attendance at some U.S. conferences over the past two years and a report released earlier in the week showing international graduate enrollment at academic medical centers down by a third.
items.strategic_implication: Academic medical centers depend on international trainees and researchers. A one-third drop in international graduate enrollment, plus conference-travel risk, threatens research staffing and future faculty pipelines. AMC leaders should review immigration legal support, travel guidance and workforce plans for international trainees.

editions.headline: Today's Healthcare Insights
editions.subheadline: A cross-source executive briefing on healthcare policy, operations, and market signals.
editions.summary_note: CMS set the 2027 Part B premium at $209.40 and reported a record $2.5 billion in Medicare savings from Shared Savings Program ACOs, while UnitedHealth became at least the 15th insurer to sue over 2027 star ratings. A federal judge dismissed Tampa General's 340B suit against Eli Lilly, big drugmakers said they will stop starting trials at PLA-linked China hospitals, and a survey found healthcare enforces AI policies less consistently than any other sector. Sources include STAT, Healthcare Dive, BioPharma Dive, KFF Health News, MedCity News, CMS, Becker's and WUSF.

editorial_buckets.name: Policy, Payment, and Regulation
editorial_buckets.synthesis: CMS set the 2027 Part B premium at $209.40, up 3.2%, and reported a record $2.5 billion in Medicare savings from Shared Savings Program ACOs, with physician-led and primary care-heavy ACOs outperforming. UnitedHealth became at least the 15th insurer to sue over 2027 star ratings. On Capitol Hill, Republicans conceded stalled PBM and drug-patent bills, and Senate Democrats are preparing to escalate their probe of the 760,000 ACA cancellations. New York opted into the work-requirement hold-harmless period, and a federal judge struck down Ryan White grant conditions on transgender care.

items.title: 2027 Medicare Part B standard premium rises 3.2% to $209.40, with a $292 deductible
items.summary: CMS's Federal Register notice sets the standard monthly Part B premium at $209.40 for 2027, $6.50 (3.2%) above 2026's $202.90, and the annual Part B deductible at $292. The premium equals 50% of the $418.70 monthly actuarial rate for aged enrollees; the disabled-enrollee actuarial rate is $452.40. Higher-income beneficiaries will pay about 35% to 85% of total Part B cost through income-related adjustments. CMS released the Part A figures and Part D income-related amounts at the same time.
items.strategic_implication: The increase is modest compared with recent years, but it lands as Medicare Advantage plans pull back benefits and Part D standalone premiums rise. Patient-financial-services and senior-market teams should update cost-share estimates and financial-assistance screening for January. Plans with Part B giveback benefits should check how the new base changes their member messaging.

items.title: Shared Savings Program ACOs post a record $2.5 billion in Medicare savings for 2025; physician-led ACOs keep outperforming
items.summary: CMS said 80% of the 472 Shared Savings Program ACOs, covering 84% of 10.9 million assigned beneficiaries, earned performance payments totaling $4.9 billion in performance year 2025, and Medicare saved $2.5 billion against benchmarks, the most in the program's history and its ninth straight year of savings. Gross per capita savings rose to $690 from $643, while Medicare's net per capita savings slipped to $234 from $241 as more ACOs moved into two-sided risk. Low-revenue ACOs, typically physician-led or built on FQHCs and rural health centers, generated $300 in net per capita savings versus $169 for hospital-led ACOs, and primary care-heavy ACOs generated $417 versus $208. CMS says the program reached a record 12.6 million beneficiaries.
items.strategic_implication: The data favors primary care-anchored, physician-led models, a useful argument for independent groups, FQHC networks and rural providers deciding whether to take on downside risk. Hospital-led ACOs should look hard at referral leakage and specialist cost drivers. Expect CMS to cite these results as it pushes more beneficiaries into accountable-care arrangements.

items.title: UnitedHealth becomes at least the 15th Medicare Advantage insurer to sue CMS over 2027 star ratings
items.summary: UnitedHealth Group, the largest Medicare Advantage insurer with more than 9 million members, sued the federal government to reverse its lowered 2027 star ratings. Plans rated at least four stars receive bonus payments, and the insurers suing argue that CMS measured performance inconsistently and pushed scores below bonus thresholds. The suit comes as Medicare's annual enrollment period runs through Dec. 7. STAT's full report is paywalled; this summary relies on the visible text.
items.strategic_implication: With the largest MA carrier now in court, the outcome could reshape 2028 bonus payments across the industry. Providers in MA value-based contracts tied to star performance should model both scenarios before year-end negotiations. Expect plans that lose bonus revenue to tighten benefits, networks or utilization management in 2028 bids.

items.title: Republicans concede two years of inaction on drug pricing as Senate Judiciary revisits stalled PBM and patent bills
items.summary: At a Senate Judiciary hearing, lawmakers from both parties called drug costs too high and pressed for PBM reform. The committee advanced six bipartisan bills last year targeting PBM self-dealing, product hopping, patent thickets and pay-for-delay deals, but only one, the Affordable Prescriptions for Patients Act limiting biologic patent suits against biosimilar makers, reached the floor. Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said, "I am embarrassed that my side has been in control for two years, and we've done nothing." Chairman Chuck Grassley cited a crowded calendar and industry pushback.
items.strategic_implication: With Democrats expected to control both chambers in January, PBM and patent reform could become a bipartisan opening, though health system pharmacy leaders should not count on it passing quickly. Employers and health plans should watch for delinking and transparency provisions that could change rebate economics in 2027-2028 contracts.

items.title: Incoming Democratic majority sets up a tougher Senate probe of the 760,000 ACA enrollment cancellations
items.summary: A dozen Democratic senators sent 28 questions to 10 insurers, including Elevance, Centene, Cigna, Oscar, Molina, Florida Blue and UnitedHealthcare, about their role in CMS's late-August cancellation of 760,000 ACA enrollments flagged as suspicious; responses were due Nov. 6. Another 419,000 enrollments remain under scrutiny. Marketplace enrollment fell to about 19 million for 2026 from nearly 22 million in 2025 after enhanced subsidies expired, and CMS says fewer than 0.01% of those purged sought reinstatement. With Democrats expected to control the Senate in January, Ron Wyden is in line to chair Finance and Bernie Sanders to chair HELP.
items.strategic_implication: Insurers face subpoena-backed oversight in 2027 over how they handled flagged enrollees, which could lead to reinstatement demands or new rules on enrollment verification. Hospitals in high-marketplace states should track coverage loss among patients and work with navigators during open enrollment, which runs into January.

items.title: New York opts into Medicaid work-requirement hold-harmless period, seeks a Bronx-wide exemption and commits $213 million to enrollment help
items.summary: New York will use CMS's optional hold-harmless period through June 30, 2027, under which states assess compliance with the H.R. 1 work requirement but do not deny or disenroll otherwise eligible people solely for not meeting it. The state also asked to exempt all Bronx residents under the law's high-unemployment hardship standard, which it says only the Bronx currently meets. It committed $213 million in total Navigator funding, including $32 million a year for 49 community organizations, and says nearly 2 million eligible New Yorkers are at risk. This follows the federal enforcement delay covered Nov. 16.
items.strategic_implication: New York offers a playbook for other expansion states: use the transition period to test systems and build outreach capacity instead of beginning terminations. Safety-net hospitals and FQHCs should coordinate with state navigators now, before enforcement starts in July 2027, and watch whether CMS approves county-level unemployment exemptions.

items.title: Federal judge strikes Ryan White HIV grant conditions barring transgender-affirming care
items.summary: U.S. District Judge William Young in Boston ruled that HRSA cannot bar providers funded by the Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program from acknowledging transgender patients' gender identity or providing gender-affirming care. In a 165-page decision after a September bench trial in a suit brought by groups including the American Academy of HIV Medicine, Young found the conditions violated the First Amendment and the Fifth Amendment's equal protection guarantee. The administration is likely to appeal.
items.strategic_implication: Ryan White-funded clinics get relief on grant terms for now, but compliance teams should not change policies until the appeal path is clear. More broadly, the ruling shows courts are scrutinizing ideology-based federal grant conditions, a recurring issue for health centers and academic medical centers.

editorial_buckets.name: Digital Health and AI
editorial_buckets.synthesis: A DNSFilter survey finds healthcare has the weakest enforcement of AI policies of any sector, and 1 in 10 respondents report an incident already caused by an unapproved AI tool. At HLTH, a BCBSA executive said AI should never make a medical-necessity denial on its own. Knit Health raised $35 million for a healthcare world model built to route patients to the right care, and Hims & Hers and Noom moved peptides into the mainstream consumer market.

items.title: Healthcare lags every sector in enforcing AI policies as shadow AI drives security incidents
items.summary: A DNSFilter survey of 30 healthcare IT and security professionals, part of a 400-manager cross-industry sample, found 70% of healthcare organizations have AI policies but only 40% enforce them consistently, the lowest of any sector. Six in 10 rely on AI and SaaS vendors to alert them to incidents, versus 43% elsewhere; 4 in 10 monitor fewer than half their security tools; and at 47%, employees can grant a new AI tool system access without higher approval. Twenty-seven percent know of unauthorized AI connections, 1 in 10 say an unapproved tool has already caused an incident, and one-third had an incident they never reported to regulators or customers. The healthcare sample is small.
items.strategic_implication: Ambient scribes, browser copilots and departmental AI purchases are growing faster than governance. CISOs and compliance officers should inventory AI and SaaS integrations, require approval before tools get access to EHR or identity systems, and make sure incidents involving third-party AI are reported under HIPAA.

items.title: BCBSA's COO says AI 'should not deny an authorization for medical necessity,' as HLTH panel debates who should decide
items.summary: At HLTH, Blue Cross Blue Shield Association COO Sean Robbins said AI can assist, but a licensed clinician should make the final call on any medical-necessity denial. Claimable CEO Dr. Warris Bokhari argued that for oncology the decision should rest with the treating physician, and alleged that Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Illinois relied on 1994-era case data to deny liver transplants for cancer patients. Dr. Mandy Cohen, national advisor at Manatt Health, called for redesigning prior authorization instead of just speeding it up, since payment incentives drive low-value requests.
items.strategic_implication: Payer leaders are publicly committing to keep a human in the loop on denials, which gives providers and regulators a standard to hold them to as AI-assisted review spreads. With CMS's electronic prior authorization API deadline on Jan. 1, revenue-cycle teams should track denial rationales and evidence citations so they can challenge outdated criteria on appeal.

items.title: Knit Health raises $35 million for a healthcare 'world model' trained on 140 million records to route patients to the right care
items.summary: Berkeley spinout Knit Health raised a $35 million Series A to commercialize Med-BEAM, a model trained on 140 million patient records that predicts patient needs and steers referrals and scheduling. CEO and health economist Jonathan Kolstad said the first three go-lives are targeted for February or March 2027, and one design partner identified 97 additional uses after starting with one. He cited rheumatology clinics booked 12 months out where one-third to one-half of patients turn out not to have rheumatologic disease. Knit is working with large systems, safety-net hospitals and now payers.
items.strategic_implication: Access and referral triage is becoming a distinct AI category, competing with Epic Cosmos-based tools. Systems with long specialty waits should test whether predictive routing frees appointment slots before adding specialist FTEs, and should ask for evidence on equity and misrouting.

items.title: Hims & Hers and Noom launch peptide prescriptions, bringing largely untested compounds to a mass market
items.summary: Hims & Hers and Noom, valued at more than $3.5 billion and $3.7 billion respectively, said they will offer peptide prescriptions to eligible patients, following smaller telehealth companies. Many consumer-marketed compounded peptides lack FDA approval and randomized human safety and efficacy data, but an HHS decision under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a peptide enthusiast, cleared the way for wider sales. STAT called the launches a "pivotal moment for peptides in the United States." The full article is paywalled.
items.strategic_implication: After GLP-1s, direct-to-consumer telehealth is moving into peptides, which are less regulated. Primary care and emergency clinicians should start asking patients about peptide use, and pharmacy and compliance leaders should watch for adverse-event signals and any change in FDA enforcement discretion.

editorial_buckets.name: Market and Industry Signals
editorial_buckets.synthesis: China is now a policy and dealmaking issue for drugmakers: five big drugmakers told House investigators they will not start trials at PLA-linked hospitals, and a congressional biotech commission warned China could 'corner' the sector. The FDA approved Regeneron's quarterly RNAi drug for myasthenia gravis at a $410,000 list price and Sanofi's first neurological Gaucher therapy. GeneDx is changing CEOs as whole-genome pricing compresses margins.

items.title: Merck, Lilly, AbbVie, Pfizer and BMS tell House China committee they will stop starting trials at PLA-linked hospitals
items.summary: The House Select Committee on China said five drugmakers, Merck, Eli Lilly, AbbVie, Pfizer and Bristol Myers Squibb, indicated they will not start new clinical studies at sites linked to the People's Liberation Army, at military-affiliated hospitals or in Xinjiang. The committee opened investigations into the companies in June, citing intellectual-property exposure, military entanglement, ethics at trial sites and security risks. STAT's full report is paywalled.
items.strategic_implication: Shifting global trial sites back toward the U.S. and allied countries could bring more industry-sponsored trial volume to U.S. academic and community research sites. Research administrators should be ready for sponsors asking about site capacity and enrollment speed, and should expect more scrutiny of foreign data in submissions.

items.title: Congressional biotech commission warns China could 'corner the sector' and endorses adding biotech to the COINS Act
items.summary: The 11-member National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology warned that China's five-year plan, which aims to produce one-quarter of the world's first-in-class drugs by 2030, could leave U.S. patients "vulnerable to supply chain weaponization." It endorsed a Treasury proposal to add biotech to the COINS Act's outbound-investment limits. BioPharma Dive counts more than 120 licensing deals between Western and Chinese drug developers since early 2025. Chair Caitlin Frazer said the deals "are starting to favor the Chinese startups." Separately, BioPharma Dive notes that China-sourced startups such as Ouro, Candid and Ollin have produced billion-dollar exits in 2026.
items.strategic_implication: Investment restrictions could slow the licensing of Chinese assets that has fed U.S. pipelines and lowered early-stage costs. Health system pharmacy and supply-chain leaders should add China-dependent ingredient and drug exposure to their risk registers, and investors should price in deal-review risk.

items.title: FDA approves Regeneron's Livsayis, the first RNAi drug for an autoimmune disease, at a $410,000 list price
items.summary: The FDA approved Livsayis (cemdisiran), an RNA interference therapy that reduces C5, for adults with AChR antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis. It is dosed by subcutaneous injection four times a year, compared with weekly dosing for AstraZeneca's newly approved Klygefa, and carries a $410,000 annual list price. Discovered by Alnylam, which earns a $25 million milestone plus royalties, it enters a crowded field with argenx and AstraZeneca. TD Cowen projects $1.5 billion in peak sales; RBC called the launch environment "relatively challenging."
items.strategic_implication: Myasthenia gravis now has several six-figure biologics competing on dosing convenience. Payers will likely use step therapy and site-of-care rules, and specialty pharmacy and infusion programs should weigh how a quarterly injection shifts volume away from infused therapies.

items.title: FDA clears Sanofi's Infilbray, the first therapy for neurological symptoms of Type 3 Gaucher disease
items.summary: Sanofi's once-daily pill Infilbray (venglustat) is approved for adults and children weighing at least 15 kg with Type 3 Gaucher disease, the first treatment for the disorder's neurological symptoms. One year of treatment improved neurological symptoms in a Phase 3 trial. The drug, acquired with Genzyme in 2011, had failed in Parkinson's, Fabry and other indications. Labeling warns of suicidal thoughts, pediatric lens clouding and fetal harm, and pricing has not been disclosed. RBC said sales expectations are modest as Sanofi prepares for Dupixent's patent loss.
items.strategic_implication: This is a first-in-class oral option for a small rare-disease population that has had no neurological treatment. Specialty pharmacies and genetic centers should plan for prior authorization and safety monitoring requirements once pricing is set.

items.title: GeneDx taps Quanterix's Everett Cunningham as CEO amid whole-genome margin pressure
items.summary: GeneDx named Everett Cunningham, who left Quanterix after less than a year, CEO effective on or before Dec. 15, succeeding Katherine Stueland, who will advise through Jan. 31. TD Cowen said sales nearly tripled under Stueland since 2021 but have been "more uneven" as price realization slowed and demand shifted to lower-margin whole genomes. Analysts pointed to Cunningham's Exact Sciences experience in building primary care channels, which represent nearly two-thirds of GeneDx's rare-disease opportunity. Quanterix named Jim Gute interim CEO.
items.strategic_implication: GeneDx's push into primary care, if it works, would bring genomic testing into general pediatric and primary care practices. Health systems should expect more vendor outreach on embedded genetic testing and should press on reimbursement, genetic counseling capacity and how results flow back into the EHR.

editorial_buckets.name: Provider Operations
editorial_buckets.synthesis: A federal judge dismissed Tampa General's 340B lawsuit against Eli Lilly, keeping manufacturers' claims-data requirements in place for now. Dallas-based Children's Health posted a 34% drop in third-quarter operating income, and Becker's November layoff tracker shows cuts concentrated in administrative, IT and health-plan roles as systems respond to reimbursement and cost pressure.

source_refs.source: KFF Health News First Edition (citing Modern Healthcare)

items.title: Judge dismisses Tampa General's 340B lawsuit against Eli Lilly over claims-data demands
items.summary: U.S. District Judge William Jung in Tampa granted Lilly's motion to dismiss Tampa General Hospital's July suit challenging the drugmaker's requirement that 340B hospitals submit prescription-level claims data through its Electronic Submission Platform. Relying largely on the Supreme Court's 2011 Astra decision, Jung found that hospitals cannot use Florida consumer-protection law to enforce 340B pricing terms. TGH said losing the discounts raised its Lilly drug costs by 25% to 50%, potentially tens of millions of dollars a year. Similar challenges are pending, including a Missouri AG action and a Massachusetts hospital suit.
items.strategic_implication: The ruling weakens one legal route for covered entities, state consumer-protection claims, and strengthens manufacturers' leverage as the federal 340B rebate pilot begins in January. 340B program leaders should model the margin hit from complying with claims-data requirements versus losing discounts, and should focus advocacy on HRSA and state 340B contract-pharmacy laws.

items.title: Children's Health operating income falls 34% in Q3, with margin dropping to 6.5% from 10.3%
items.summary: Dallas-based Children's Health reported third-quarter 2026 operating income of $168.2 million, a 6.5% margin, down from $253.3 million and a 10.3% margin a year earlier, according to its Nov. 19 financial report. Becker's details are drawn from the visible summary.
items.strategic_implication: Becker's summary does not give the drivers, but the drop shows that even strong pediatric systems are vulnerable as Medicaid-heavy payer mixes face H.R. 1 pressure. Pediatric CFOs should stress-test 2027 budgets for Medicaid enrollment losses and supplemental-payment changes.

items.title: November layoffs concentrate in administrative, IT and health-plan roles at Keck, RWJBarnabas, Presbyterian and others
items.summary: Becker's tracker shows a wave of non-clinical cuts this month. Keck Medicine of USC is laying off 77 people, including five C-suite executives, from Dec. 7 to Jan. 8 with more reductions expected; RWJBarnabas Health will eliminate 106 positions in February; Presbyterian Healthcare Services is cutting about 135, mostly health-plan roles, after exiting most Medicare Advantage plans for 2027; Kootenai Health is eliminating 80 positions, citing a $60 million increase in annual drug costs; and Ascension will close an insurance unit and lay off 51. Children's Mercy cut 115 positions and outsourced 473 revenue-cycle and scheduling staff.
items.strategic_implication: Systems are cutting overhead first, specifically management layers, IT and provider-sponsored plan operations, rather than bedside staff. Executives planning similar moves should weigh the morale risk shown in Bain's latest physician survey and be clear about which functions automation or outsourcing will absorb.

editorial_buckets.name: Workforce & Clinical Practice
editorial_buckets.synthesis: Bain's physician survey shows engagement at its lowest since 2017, with respect and recognition replacing burnout as the main reason physicians cite for wanting to leave. A National Academies report calling for faster retractions was pulled before release over suspect citations. Brain-implant trial participants are pressing for post-trial support and access to their neural data, and an infant malaria study warns that combining a monoclonal antibody with vaccines may reduce vaccine response.

items.title: Bain: 25% of physicians are weighing an exit, and lack of respect, not burnout, is now the top non-pay driver
items.summary: Bain's US Front Line of Healthcare 2026 report, based on a June survey of 400 physicians plus nurses and administrators, found physician employee Net Promoter Score fell from 33 in 2024 to 6, the lowest since 2017. A quarter of physicians are considering switching employers, up 5 points, and those in management-led organizations are more than twice as likely to leave as those in physician-led settings. Physicians who feel involved in decisions score 88 points higher. Fifty-five percent of administrators say physician recruiting has gotten harder, up from 35% in 2024. The report was released Nov. 16 and was not covered in earlier editions.
items.strategic_implication: Retention is increasingly about governance, not just pay. CMOs and CEOs should formalize physician decision rights on scheduling, AI tool selection and service-line strategy. Bain says AI investments will not pay off if clinicians feel left out of the decisions.

items.title: National Academies urges 12-week retraction timelines, then pauses its own report over apparently fabricated citations
items.summary: A 157-page National Academies report chaired by Randy Schekman calls on journals to resolve research-integrity concerns within 12 weeks, or six months for complex cases, and says authors who cannot produce original data could face retraction. More than 5,000 studies were retracted in 2025, on average about 2.4 years after publication, as annual output grew to 6.7 million articles. The Academies paused publication after Science reported that 10 references appeared to contain fabricated co-author names, possibly from a large language model; no new release date has been set.
items.strategic_implication: The irony is the lesson: AI-assisted drafting is getting into high-stakes evidence documents. Research offices, journal editors and clinical guideline committees should verify references and disclose AI use before anything is published.

items.title: Brain-implant trial participants push for post-trial support and ownership of their neural data
items.summary: The BCI Pioneers Coalition released 13 recommendations for startups, researchers and regulators covering post-trial care, informed consent and neural-data privacy. Co-founder Ian Burkhart, implanted at Ohio State in 2014, said a proposed device removal during a funding gap made him feel "more akin to a lab rat versus being a human," and called for participants to be able to access and share their own neural data. UCLA ethicist Anna Wexler said there are no good solutions yet for long-term support, despite discussion of insurance, escrows and institutional commitments.
items.strategic_implication: As BCI trials grow, after Synchron's recent pause, IRBs and sponsors will face pressure to fund long-term device support and define data rights at enrollment. Academic medical centers hosting neurotech trials should add explicit post-trial obligations to their contracts.

items.title: Malaria monoclonal L9LS is 78% effective in Mali infants but appears to reduce R21 vaccine antibody responses
items.summary: In a study of infants 1 to 12 months old in Mali presented at the ASTMH annual meeting, the long-acting monoclonal antibody L9LS was 78% effective against malaria versus placebo over a six-month transmission season. When given after R21 vaccination, however, it was associated with 20% to 30% lower vaccine-generated antibody levels, and the clinical significance is unclear. NIAID's Robert Seder said pivotal trials, hoped to begin in 2028, will focus first on other groups such as pregnant people and children recovering after malaria hospitalization. Malaria killed about 610,000 people in 2024.
items.strategic_implication: Global health funders will need to sequence monoclonals and vaccines carefully. For U.S. audiences, the finding is a reminder that layering preventives, as with RSV antibodies and maternal vaccines, needs interaction data before it becomes standard practice.

editions.headline: Today's Healthcare Insights
editions.subheadline: A cross-source executive briefing on healthcare policy, operations, and market signals.
editions.summary_note: Only 1 in 10 payers say they are ready for CMS's Jan. 1 electronic prior authorization API deadline, and the Labor Department proposed ending the Schedule A green card fast track for foreign nurses and physical therapists. Minnesota cleared Sutter's Allina deal with $2.15 billion in commitments, Epic promised easier AI access to its records, and Abridge is offering its clinical Assistant free to community health centers, while NACHC warns up to 1,800 sites could close. Sources include STAT, Healthcare Dive, BioPharma Dive, MedCity News, Becker's, Fierce Healthcare and NBC News.
