Fierce Healthcare and Becker's RSS returned bot-check pages and were not parsed; their articles were reached through web search.

STAT+ articles (O'Neill/NSF, FDA post-Overton, USPSTF, Epic at HLTH, MAHA PAC, Merck-Isomorphic, STREAM column) were paywalled; items rely on visible text, STAT Morning Rounds and corroborating coverage.
source_run.run_notes: 21 items cover developments reported from midday Nov. 18 through the morning of Nov. 19. Checked against the prior 30 editions for repeats; excluded the CMS CRUSH anti-fraud proposed rule (covered Nov. 17), compounded GLP-1 debate and medical school redesign (covered Nov. 18), measles elimination loss (Nov. 16) and recurring flu-activity updates. The Summit, Medicare fee-schedule and FDA leadership items are new developments that follow earlier coverage. Screened but not itemized: Erasca KRAS preview (data embargoed until Nov. 20), NIH chimpanzee relocation, KFF Social Security early-claims analysis, Pharmalittle roundups and KFF reader letters.

editorial_buckets.name: Policy, Payment, and Regulation
editorial_buckets.synthesis: Payers are largely unready for CMS's Jan. 1 electronic prior authorization API deadline, and Medicare's 20% same-day exam-plus-procedure cut could split visits starting the same day. A reconstituted USPSTF meets for the first time in over a year, and Cassidy's cancellation of the O'Neill NSF vote, a day after the Overton withdrawal, leaves FDA without a permanent leader into 2027. Democrats are coalescing around Medicare eligibility at 55, and MAHA's PAC spent little on its candidates.

items.title: Six weeks out, only 1 in 10 payers say they are fully ready for CMS's Jan. 1, 2027 electronic prior authorization API deadline
items.summary: A WEDI survey found just 10% of government-regulated payers are completely ready to stand up the prior authorization and data-sharing APIs required under CMS's 2024 interoperability rule by Jan. 1, 2027. Nearly two-thirds are at least halfway there, but 17% have not started, and 62% said the work has cost more than expected; none said less. Providers are not required to build the APIs, yet fewer than 10% have fully implemented them, one-fifth have not started, and nearly three-quarters said payer readiness is very or extremely important. CMS estimates payer costs at $182 million in year one and up to $1.6 billion over a decade.
items.strategic_implication: Expect an uneven go-live: some Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care and exchange plans will meet the date, others will rely on workarounds. Provider revenue-cycle leaders should confirm, payer by payer, which APIs will actually be live in January, line up ONC/CMS testing partners now, and avoid assuming fax and portal volume drops on day one.

items.title: Medicare's 20% same-day exam-plus-procedure cut takes effect Jan. 1, and specialists warn patients may need two visits
items.summary: Under the 2027 Medicare physician fee schedule finalized Nov. 4, when a physician bills a separately identifiable office visit with modifier 25 on the same day as a minor procedure with a zero-day global period, Medicare will pay the lower-valued service at 20% less. The cut applies only to the same physician or same specialty in the same group, so different specialists seeing a patient the same day are paid in full. CMS says it was paying twice for overlapping intake and room work; some specialists, notably in dermatology and orthopedics, say they may split exams and injections or biopsies into separate appointments. The same rule lowers conversion-factor-based rates by 1.83% for APM participants and 2.31% for everyone else.
items.strategic_implication: This follows the Nov. 5 fee-schedule item with the operational effect now coming into focus. Practices with heavy injection or biopsy volume should model the revenue impact by provider and decide on scheduling policy before January rather than letting it drift; health systems should watch for access complaints, added copays for patients, and slot capacity strain if visits split.

items.title: Reconstituted USPSTF meets this week for the first time in more than a year, with cervical cancer, perinatal depression and alcohol screening on the agenda
items.summary: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, whose A and B grades determine which preventive services most insurers must cover without cost sharing, is scheduled to meet this week for the first time in more than a year, according to an AHRQ notice sent Nov. 18. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. canceled meetings last year and overhauled the panel's membership, leaving several recommendations awaiting finalization. The agenda covers cervical cancer screening, perinatal depression and unhealthy alcohol use in teens and adults, each not updated in at least five years, plus an evidence presentation on healthy lifestyles to prevent cardiovascular disease, expert presentations on chronic kidney disease, colorectal and lung cancer screening, and a discussion of task force methods.
items.strategic_implication: Restarting the pipeline matters more than any single vote: new grades flow into ACA no-cost coverage mandates. Payer benefit teams and population-health leaders should track the cervical cancer and perinatal depression outputs and the 'task force methods' discussion, which could signal how the reconstituted panel will weigh evidence going forward.

items.title: Cassidy cancels vote on Jim O'Neill for NSF a day after the FDA nomination collapse, leaving FDA leaderless into 2027
items.summary: Senate HELP Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) canceled the committee vote on former HHS and CDC official Jim O'Neill's nomination to lead the National Science Foundation, saying O'Neill lacked support and 'did not do enough to stand up for science' against Secretary Kennedy's decisions. It came a day after the White House withdrew Heidi Overton's FDA nomination. FDA has had no permanent commissioner since May; acting commissioner Kyle Diamantas reportedly does not want the job and may leave after the new year, and Congress is unlikely to confirm a nominee before January, when Democrats take Senate control. User-fee reauthorization is the next big FDA test.
items.strategic_implication: Two failed health-science nominations in two days signal that the lame-duck Senate will not rubber-stamp HHS-aligned picks. For drug, device and diagnostics sponsors, plan for continued acting leadership at FDA through at least early 2027 and a user-fee reauthorization negotiated with a Democratic Senate.

items.title: Sanders predicts Medicare eligibility at 55 can pass under Trump, with Wyden and Jeffries aligned on 'Medicare for More'
items.summary: At a Nov. 18 press conference, Sen. Bernie Sanders said Democrats will pass legislation lowering Medicare eligibility while President Trump is in office and that he is 'not absolutely certain that Trump would not sign it.' His plan would lower the eligibility age from 65 to 55, add dental, vision and hearing coverage, and guarantee free Medicaid coverage to children through age 19. Sen. Ron Wyden, expected to lead the committee with jurisdiction, supports it, and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries backs 'Medicare for More' and 'Medikids.' Sanders also signaled oversight of Secretary Kennedy, insurers and drug pricing if he chairs HELP.
items.strategic_implication: Treat this as an agenda-setting marker for 2027 rather than near-term law, but it reframes the debate from 'Medicare for All' to incremental age-band expansion. Hospitals and MA plans should model the payer-mix effect of shifting 55-to-64 commercial lives to Medicare rates, and expect aggressive HELP oversight hearings on pharma and insurers.

items.title: STAT investigation: MAHA PAC had more than $10 million but spent little on candidates before midterm losses
items.summary: A STAT review of filings found the MAHA PAC led by Tony Lyons had more than $10 million to spend through the cycle but directed most of it to allies, boosters, pundits and an affiliated nonprofit rather than to races. It spent less than $50,000 on a California House race it had called a priority. After a string of MAHA candidate losses, Lyons told supporters the movement was up against 'some of the most powerful and best funded interests in the world.'
items.strategic_implication: MAHA's electoral weakness, alongside the Overton and O'Neill setbacks, suggests the movement's leverage in Congress is shrinking even as it keeps influence inside HHS. Food, beverage, vaccine and pharma stakeholders should expect MAHA priorities to advance mainly through administrative action rather than legislation in 2027.

editorial_buckets.name: Digital Health and AI
editorial_buckets.synthesis: HLTH week is defining the next phase of clinical AI: Epic publicly promised easier AI access to its records, Abridge is offering its clinical Assistant free to 108,000 health center clinicians and adding local pathways, and Suki is backing a new agentic platform with outcome guarantees. Leaders debated how far AI can stretch primary care panels.

items.title: Epic answers STAT's competition investigation at HLTH and promises easier AI access to its records
items.summary: Speaking on a STAT stage at HLTH in Las Vegas, Epic executives responded publicly for the first time to a STAT investigation finding the company selectively withheld data access from rival app developers. EVP of R&D Seth Howard said Epic received about 75,000 data-access inquiries last year for systems holding records on more than 280 million Americans, and that building bespoke connections for each is not feasible. Executives said Epic will make it easier for companies to use AI to read data stored on its platform and is working toward a more open ecosystem.
items.strategic_implication: A public commitment from Epic gives health systems leverage. CIOs negotiating with third-party AI vendors should ask Epic for specific, dated access paths (APIs, scopes, pricing) rather than general assurances, and track whether information-blocking scrutiny at ONC and the FTC builds on this record.

items.title: Abridge offers its clinical Assistant free to 108,000 community health center clinicians and adds local care pathways and Cochrane evidence
items.summary: Abridge said its Assistant clinical agent, already deployed across more than 300 health systems and more than 75 VA medical centers, where it answered more than 40,000 clinician questions last month, will be available at no cost to 108,000 clinicians at National Association of Community Health Centers member sites serving about 52 million people. A new opt-in Local Pathways feature lets the Assistant cite a health system's own care pathways alongside patient context, and Wiley will license nearly 10,000 Cochrane systematic reviews and about 4,000 Cochrane Clinical Answers to the tool. Viz.ai and Wolters Kluwer announced a similar UpToDate integration.
items.strategic_implication: Ambient-scribe vendors are racing to become the point-of-care decision-support layer. Health systems should treat local-pathway features as a governance project: someone must own, version and retire the pathways the AI cites. The free FQHC offer also expands AI access in rural and safety-net settings, which can help close gaps in clinical decision support.

items.title: Suki launches 'Suki OS' agentic layer with prior authorization and documentation agents and offers fee refunds if outcomes miss
items.summary: AI scribe company Suki launched Suki OS, a platform connecting existing health software and AI agents, with new agents for prior authorization and clinical documentation that can prepare pre-visit summaries, verify insurance and support revenue-cycle work. CEO Punit Singh Soni said 'ambient documentation is a starting point, not the destination.' Suki says it will return customer fees if agreed performance outcomes are not met, though it did not disclose targets. Competitors include Abridge and Ambience; partners include Optum and Wolters Kluwer's UpToDate.
items.strategic_implication: Outcome-guarantee pricing is becoming a buying lever in ambient AI. Procurement teams should push vendors to define measurable targets (denial rates, prior auth turnaround, after-hours documentation time) and clawback terms in contracts, and avoid stacking overlapping agent platforms from multiple scribe vendors.

items.title: HLTH leaders debate how far AI can stretch primary care capacity, from 1,500 to 2,500 patients per clinician
items.summary: With about one-third of Americans lacking a primary care provider and only one-fourth of new doctors entering the field, HLTH speakers described AI as a way to extend primary care capacity. NACHC CEO Dr. Kyu Rhee said AI could let him manage 2,500 patients rather than 1,500 with a team of 11; Counsel Health, which Oura agreed to buy for $625 million, described its clinician-supervised AI as 'almost an Iron Man suit.' AMA CEO Dr. John Whyte pushed back that 'patients don't want to hear a cancer diagnosis from an LLM,' and Anthropic's Dr. Sarah Russell pointed to AI's role in routing patients.
items.strategic_implication: Panel-size expansion claims will soon show up in workforce and staffing models. Primary care leaders should pilot AI-supported triage and asynchronous care with clear escalation rules and measure panel size, quality and patient experience before adjusting staffing ratios or productivity expectations.

editorial_buckets.name: Market and Industry Signals
editorial_buckets.synthesis: Minnesota cleared Sutter's acquisition of Allina with $2.15 billion in binding commitments, a template for conditional approval of cross-market mergers. Pfizer joined the in vivo CAR-T race through a China deal, FDA's published Summit letter reset the bar for China-originated oncology data, Merck signed with Isomorphic, and Hone Health raised $228 million for cash-pay longevity care.

items.title: Minnesota AG clears Sutter Health's Allina acquisition with a 10-year agreement and $2.15 billion investment commitment
items.summary: Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison announced a 10-year oversight agreement with Sutter Health and Allina Health that clears the deal to close around Jan. 1. Sutter will invest $2.15 billion in Minnesota, with at least $150 million going to rural care and rural residency programs, and the systems agreed to keep Allina's core services and gender and reproductive care for five years, stay in Medicare and Medicaid, and honor existing labor contracts. The combined $26 billion system will have 39 hospitals and about 88,000 employees across California, Minnesota and Wisconsin. Allina reported nearly $1 billion in operating losses over five years.
items.strategic_implication: This is a template for how state AGs are approving cross-market mergers: binding service-line, rural-investment and labor conditions in exchange for clearance. Systems pursuing out-of-state partners should expect similar multi-year commitments and price in compliance reporting. Competitors in the Twin Cities should prepare for a better-capitalized Allina.

items.title: Pfizer pays $330 million up front for China-based Starna's in vivo CAR-T programs in autoimmune disease
items.summary: Pfizer will pay Starna Therapeutics $330 million up front and up to $2.3 billion in milestones, plus royalties, for ex-Greater China rights to three preclinical in vivo cell therapy programs for autoimmune disease and rights to use Starna's RNA technology in inflammation, immunology and oncology. It is Pfizer's first move into in vivo CAR-T and at least its fifth major alliance with a Chinese company since the start of 2025. In vivo approaches aim to reprogram immune cells inside the body, avoiding the lengthy manufacturing and chemotherapy conditioning of ex vivo CAR-T; AstraZeneca, AbbVie, Gilead, Bristol Myers Squibb and Eli Lilly have made similar acquisitions.
items.strategic_implication: If in vivo CAR-T works, cell therapy could shift from specialized academic centers to a much broader site-of-care footprint, including for lupus and MS. Health systems building cell therapy programs should watch this class before overcommitting to ex vivo apheresis and manufacturing infrastructure; the steady flow of China-sourced assets also keeps U.S. biosecurity policy in play.

items.title: FDA publishes rejection letter for Summit's ivonescimab, calling benefits 'modest' and advising a new trial
items.summary: FDA released the complete response letter rejecting Summit Therapeutics and Akeso's ivonescimab for lung cancer, citing concerns about the size of its effect on tumor progression, the relevance of the largely non-U.S. data to American patients and the lack of a clear survival benefit; it said the 'modest' benefits do not outweigh added safety risks and advised a new trial. A Leerink analyst said a new application alone is 'unlikely to change the approval outcome.' Separately, FDA approved GSK's Nelkarmi for previously treated ALK-positive lung cancer, the second approval from its $10.6 billion Nuvalent purchase, and AstraZeneca's self-administered C5 inhibitor Klygefa for generalized myasthenia gravis.
items.strategic_implication: This follows the Nov. 16 rejection item with FDA's reasoning now public. The letter reinforces that overall survival and U.S.-relevant populations remain the bar for China-originated oncology assets, which affects licensing valuations and trial design for the many China-sourced deals now in U.S. pipelines.

items.title: Merck partners with Isomorphic Labs on AI-designed small molecules for an undisclosed oncology target
items.summary: Merck and Isomorphic Labs announced a research collaboration on Nov. 19 to discover small-molecule candidates against an undisclosed oncology target that Merck called of 'strategic importance.' The partnership pairs Isomorphic's drug-design engine, built on Nobel-winning protein-structure modeling, with Merck's existing wet-lab data; Merck will handle development, manufacturing and commercialization. Financial terms were not disclosed in the visible text. The deal follows Isomorphic's $5 billion-plus Series C covered Nov. 18.
items.strategic_implication: Large pharma is now feeding proprietary experimental data into AI design engines on high-priority targets, not just exploratory ones. The competitive edge is shifting to who owns high-quality proprietary datasets, which is relevant for academic medical centers and health systems weighing data-licensing partnerships with pharma and AI firms.

items.title: Hone Health raises $228 million, mostly growth financing, to scale direct-to-consumer longevity care and launch a peptide program
items.summary: Direct-to-consumer longevity company Hone Health, which says it has served more than 200,000 patients, raised $228 million: $28 million in Series A equity led by MarcyPen Capital Partners and $200 million in growth financing from General Catalyst's Customer Value Fund. Plans include metabolic health, inflammation and immunity programs, MRI and gut-microbiome diagnostics, AI personalization, a physician-supervised peptide program and clinical-trials infrastructure. It also launched Hone Black, a concierge membership with testing of more than 1,600 biomarkers.
items.strategic_implication: Cash-pay longevity and hormone platforms are drawing large structured financing, pulling commercially insured, higher-income patients toward subscription models outside traditional primary care. The peptide program lands amid shifting FDA compounding policy, a regulatory risk worth watching for any system considering partnerships with these platforms.

editorial_buckets.name: Provider Operations
editorial_buckets.synthesis: NACHC warns up to 1,800 health center sites could close under H.R. 1 pressures, which would shift volume to hospitals. Delaware's CON board blocked ChristianaCare's micro-hospitals after incumbent opposition, while Atrium is investing $387 million to expand pediatric capacity in a fast-growing market.

items.title: NACHC warns up to 1,800 health center sites could close and pitches a 'triple double' for primary care
items.summary: NACHC CEO Dr. Kyu Rhee told Chief Healthcare Executive at HLTH that the average community health center runs a negative 1% to 2% margin and nearly half have less than 90 days of cash on hand. Citing H.R. 1 Medicaid cuts and rising ACA premiums that could add 4 million uninsured patients, NACHC projects up to 1,800 sites could close and 34,000 jobs could be lost. Health centers serve 52 million people, including one in three rural residents. Rhee's 'triple double' calls for doubling primary care's share of spending from 5% to 10%, the share of people served at health centers from 10% to 20%, and the share of graduates entering primary care from 20% to 40%.
items.strategic_implication: Health center closures push uninsured and Medicaid patients toward hospital EDs. Hospitals, especially in rural and safety-net markets, should identify which local FQHCs are financially fragile and consider specialty-access, referral or shared-staffing partnerships now, before closures shift volume and uncompensated care onto the hospital.

items.title: Delaware certificate-of-need board rejects ChristianaCare's $123 million micro-hospital campuses after Bayhealth opposition
items.summary: Delaware's Health Resources Board on Nov. 18 denied ChristianaCare's applications for two health campuses with micro-hospitals in Camden (Kent County) and Georgetown (Sussex County), a combined $123.2 million investment. Bayhealth opposed the inpatient components, arguing that existing systems' expansions, including its own, will meet inpatient demand and that new investment should focus on outpatient care.
items.strategic_implication: Certificate-of-need and similar boards remain a real barrier to growth into a competitor's backyard, and incumbents are winning by framing the need as outpatient rather than inpatient. Systems planning micro-hospital or neighborhood-hospital strategies in CON states should lead with outpatient-first designs and documented local access gaps.

items.title: Atrium Health commits $387 million to expand Levine Children's Hospital to about 350 beds as regional pediatric volume rises 43%
items.summary: Atrium Health, part of Advocate Health, announced a $387 million expansion of Levine Children's Hospital in Charlotte, its largest capital investment since opening in 2007. The project adds more than 60 inpatient pediatric beds and more than 40 NICU beds, bringing capacity to about 350, more than doubles emergency department and surgical/procedural space, and adds a dedicated pediatric imaging center. Greater Charlotte pediatric inpatient volume is up 43% in five years, and the hospital serves children from 96 of North Carolina's 100 counties.
items.strategic_implication: While many systems close pediatric units, high-growth Sun Belt markets are going the other way and consolidating pediatric care into regional hubs. Community hospitals in those regions should plan transfer agreements and pediatric readiness around a stronger regional destination, and children's hospitals elsewhere can use the volume data to support their own capacity cases.

editorial_buckets.name: Workforce & Clinical Practice
editorial_buckets.synthesis: The Labor Department's proposal to end Schedule A would slow international nurse and PT recruitment, about 23,800 petitions a year. A cardiologist urges caution on the STREAM statin-deprescribing results, and a veteran physician's account shows what ambient AI can do for after-hours burnout.

items.title: Labor Department proposes ending Schedule A, the fast-track green card pathway for foreign nurses and physical therapists
items.summary: A Labor Department proposed rule published in the Federal Register Nov. 17 would eliminate Schedule A, the 30-plus-year exemption that lets employers sponsor professional nurses and physical therapists for green cards without first running the PERM labor-market test. DOL said it 'no longer possesses evidence' of a nationwide shortage and lacks statutory authority for occupation-wide exemptions. About 23,800 petitions a year would be affected (23,521 in FY2025). Employers would instead have to advertise for at least 90 days online, finish recruitment 30 to 60 days before filing, and would be barred from filing for two years after laying off U.S. workers in similar roles in the area. Comments are due Jan. 19, 2027.
items.strategic_implication: International nurse recruitment pipelines would get slower and more expensive, hitting rural hospitals, nursing homes and rehab providers hardest. CNOs and HR leaders should inventory pending and planned Schedule A sponsorships, accelerate filings that can be made under current rules, check whether recent layoffs would trigger the two-year bar, and consider submitting comments with local vacancy data.

items.title: Cardiologist urges caution on the STREAM statin-deprescribing trial: 'noninferior' but still worse
items.summary: The STREAM trial, presented at the American Heart Association's annual meeting, found older adults without prior heart attack or stroke who stopped statins did not have significantly different outcomes from those who continued. In a STAT column, Northwestern preventive cardiologist Vishal Khetpal notes the event curves diverged and that deprescribing was technically noninferior by the trial's prespecified margin 'but nevertheless, still inferior.' The data safety monitoring board advised patients who had stopped statins to talk with their doctors about resuming them.
items.strategic_implication: Deprescribing in older adults is a legitimate quality and polypharmacy goal, but STREAM is not a green light for blanket statin discontinuation protocols. Medical directors and pharmacy and therapeutics committees should hold off on embedding statin-stop prompts in geriatric or MA care-management workflows until full results and guideline commentary are out.

items.title: Veteran family physician: ambient AI took back the evenings EHR work had consumed for 20 years
items.summary: In a MedCity News essay, retired family physician Dr. Michael Miller, a former chief of quality and physician advocacy for Ascension St. Thomas, describes how ambient AI documentation ended a 20-year routine of finishing notes at home until 9 or 10 p.m. He cites research estimating family physicians spend about 86 minutes on EHR work each night, a projected shortage of up to 124,000 physicians by 2034, nearly half in primary care, and burnout that reached 60% in 2024 and remains above half. His advice to colleagues: 'whatever tools exist to get your evenings back, use them now.'
items.strategic_implication: Pair this account with hard metrics. Systems deploying ambient AI should measure after-hours EHR time and retention intent, not just note-completion speed, because getting time back is the benefit most likely to keep late-career physicians practicing.

editions.headline: Today's Healthcare Insights
editions.subheadline: A cross-source executive briefing on healthcare policy, operations, and market signals.
editions.summary_note: HHS finalized a HIPAA update requiring 15-day record access and delivery to patient-chosen apps, and the White House withdrew Heidi Overton's FDA nomination before her committee vote. CMS's clinical AI roadmap points to outcome-based payment, Optum is selling New York practices to Northwell and Westchester Medical Center, Baylor Scott & White's plan is dropping most prior authorizations, and Leapfrog's fall grades named three 'F' hospitals. Sources include STAT, KFF Health News, Healthcare Dive, BioPharma Dive, MedCity News and Becker's.

editorial_buckets.name: Policy, Payment, and Regulation
editorial_buckets.synthesis: HHS finalized a HIPAA update that halves record-access deadlines to 15 days and requires delivery to patient-chosen apps, while the White House pulled its FDA nominee on the eve of a committee vote. A JAMA study shows weight-loss GLP-1 use collapsed in Medicaid programs that ended coverage, CMS approved culturally specific waiver benefits for Utah and Maine, and Sen. Collins's defeat complicates the fight over political oversight of research grants.

items.title: HHS finalizes HIPAA Privacy Rule update: 15-day record access and required delivery to patient-chosen health apps
items.summary: HHS's Office for Civil Rights finalized changes to the HIPAA Privacy Rule on Nov. 16, with Federal Register publication expected this week and an effective date 60 days later; providers, payers and business associates would need to comply around July 10. The deadline to answer patient record requests drops from 30 calendar days to 15, and covered entities must send records to a qualifying personal health app when a patient asks. The rule bars unreasonable identity-verification steps such as requiring in-person visits when remote verification is available, and requires organizations to post record-access fees online. HHS estimates $784 million in first-year costs and $703 million in annual net savings in years two through five, mostly from dropping the signed privacy-notice acknowledgment.
items.strategic_implication: Release-of-information is now a compliance clock, not a back-office queue. Health systems and plans should map current turnaround times against the 15-day standard, confirm their ROI vendor contracts and patient portal/API workflows can push records to third-party apps, and post fee schedules before the July compliance date. OCR has already acted against 55 organizations for slow access, so enforcement risk is real.

items.title: White House pulls Heidi Overton's FDA commissioner nomination on the eve of the Senate HELP vote
items.summary: The White House withdrew Heidi Overton's nomination to lead FDA late Nov. 17, a day before the Senate HELP Committee's scheduled vote, amid concerns she lacked enough Republican support on the panel. Her nomination had drawn fire from MAHA figures over her role in a policy loosening standards for fruit-flavored vapes, and more than 2,500 physicians had urged rejection over vaccine-policy and telehealth abortion positions. HELP Chair Bill Cassidy said she had the votes and that the White House "abandoned a viable confirmation path." The same week, NIH named a permanent NIAID director and the president nominated Eric Ueland as comptroller general, the official who appoints MedPAC and MACPAC members.
items.strategic_implication: FDA now heads into 2027 without a confirmed commissioner, after Makary's resignation, a staffing shortage of more than 1,000 open jobs and the shelving of the priority-voucher program. Expect slower, less predictable policy calls on drugs, devices and AI tools; manufacturers and health-system pharmacy and supply-chain leaders should plan for review delays. The GAO nomination also matters to providers because MedPAC and MACPAC recommendations shape Medicare and Medicaid payment rates.

items.title: JAMA study: weight-loss GLP-1 prescriptions fell 84% in four Medicaid programs that dropped coverage
items.summary: A University of Pittsburgh study published Nov. 16 in JAMA compared California, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania and South Carolina, which ended Medicaid coverage of weight-loss GLP-1s on Jan. 1, with 10 states that kept coverage. Prescriptions fell from 2,914 to 421 per 100,000 beneficiaries between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first quarter of 2026, with declines ranging from 60.8% in South Carolina to 95.5% in Pennsylvania. The authors estimate 175,500 to 526,600 fewer beneficiaries filled prescriptions, with no significant shift to diabetes-labeled GLP-1s. California cut Medi-Cal coverage after projecting costs would reach $800 million by fiscal 2028-29; 17 state programs have added optional coverage since 2022.
items.strategic_implication: Coverage decisions, not clinical guidelines, are driving obesity treatment for low-income patients. Safety-net systems and Medicaid managed care plans in states that cut coverage should expect pent-up demand to show up in downstream cardiometabolic utilization, and should track whether patients shift to compounded or cash-pay channels. Combined with CVS's estimated $350 break-even price, the data gives states a reference point for revisiting coverage at lower net prices.

items.title: CMS approves Native American traditional-healing Medicaid waivers for Utah and Maine while denying full federal match for urban Indian clinics
items.summary: The administration approved Utah's and Maine's Medicaid waivers to cover Native American traditional healing, bringing the number of states with such waivers to six alongside Arizona, California, New Mexico and Oregon. The benefit lets Native health providers bill Medicaid for practices such as sweat lodge ceremonies, which Maine's Mi'kmaq Nation has used in opioid recovery. CMS rejected Utah's request for 100% federal reimbursement at urban Indian health organizations, even though about 87% of Native Americans live outside tribal areas. California's broader waiver, which includes traditional healing, expires at the end of December with renewal pending and a 700-page CMS letter directing alignment with federal Medicaid changes.
items.strategic_implication: The approvals show CMS will still back targeted, culturally specific waiver benefits even as it narrows Medicaid elsewhere. For tribal, urban Indian and safety-net partners, the funding gap at urban clinics limits how far the benefit can scale. States with pending 1115 renewals, especially California, should expect CMS to require alignment with the new federal work-requirement and eligibility rules as a condition of approval.

items.title: Collins's defeat leaves science advocates without a key appropriations ally as the FY2027 HHS bill omits a block on political grant oversight
items.summary: Sen. Susan Collins, chair of Senate Appropriations, lost her Maine race to Democrat Troy Jackson, and science advocates worry the loss weakens their ability to push back on administration research policy. Senate HHS spending bills released Nov. 16 did not include language blocking a White House proposal to put all federal research awards under more political oversight, though Collins told STAT she intends to block the rule before funding measures are final. STAT's Morning Rounds reports the fiscal 2027 HHS bill adds $500 million for NIH research.
items.strategic_implication: Academic medical centers should treat the lame-duck appropriations window as the main chance to shape grant-oversight rules and NIH funding levels for 2027. Research-intensive systems should keep contingency plans for award delays and indirect-cost pressure, and coordinate advocacy through AAMC and state delegations before the new Congress is seated.

editorial_buckets.name: Digital Health and AI
editorial_buckets.synthesis: CMS's clinical AI roadmap signals that future reimbursement will reward measurable outcomes, with a push for a national regulatory standard. Point-of-care integration is advancing through Viz.ai and UpToDate, but EHR consolidation at Northwell, weak follow-up for AI eye screening and low agentic-AI benchmark scores show that adoption still stalls at workflow and evaluation.

items.title: CMS roadmap for clinical 'super intelligence' points to outcome-based AI payment models and a national regulatory standard
items.summary: CMS released a non-binding roadmap on Nov. 13 laying out the administration's plan to accelerate clinical AI, which it calls clinical super intelligence. Proposals include outcome-based payments for chronic care and prevention, AI-led accountable care and total-cost-of-care arrangements building on the ACCESS, AHEAD and LEAD models, possible AI delivery of parts of the Medicare annual wellness visit, and state partnerships on AI payment models, including in Medicaid. On regulation, it favors a national standard over state-by-state rules, risk-based oversight, post-market surveillance, and a "better than today" safety bar with staged deployment that prioritizes low-risk uses.
items.strategic_implication: This is the clearest signal yet of where federal AI reimbursement is headed: payment will follow measurable outcomes, not software use. Health systems and ACOs should inventory AI tools that can show cost or quality impact in chronic care and wellness visits, and position for ACCESS-style or state Medicaid pilots. Watch for federal preemption fights with states that have passed their own AI-in-healthcare laws.

items.title: Viz.ai embeds UpToDate Expert AI into its care-coordination platform used in 2,000 U.S. hospitals
items.summary: Viz.ai and Wolters Kluwer Health announced at HLTH that UpToDate Expert AI will be integrated into Viz.ai One, letting clinicians ask clinical questions and get evidence-based answers informed by patient data without leaving their workflow. The tool cites its sources and provides information rather than decisions. Viz.ai says its platform is used in 2,000 U.S. hospitals; a 2023 study at one stroke center found door-to-groin times fell 39% for off-hours large vessel occlusion patients after deployment.
items.strategic_implication: Clinical reference content is moving into the point of care rather than sitting in a separate app. Systems already running Viz.ai for stroke and other service lines should evaluate how the integration fits their existing UpToDate licenses and AI governance policies, including how sourced answers are logged and audited.

items.title: Northwell retires its homegrown Nora clinical assistant after moving 21 hospitals onto Epic
items.summary: Northwell Health retired Nora, an internally built assistant that pushed patient data to clinicians' mobile devices for rounds and diabetes management, after its early-November Wave 3 go-live moved 21 legacy hospitals and more than 800 ambulatory sites onto Epic. The roughly $1.2 billion project is consolidating more than 30 legacy EHRs across the 28-hospital system, with full transition targeted by 2030. Functions such as mobile interdisciplinary rounds will move to Epic's Haiku app.
items.strategic_implication: EHR consolidation often retires homegrown innovation. Systems building custom AI or workflow tools on top of legacy platforms should plan exit paths and capture lessons before a migration, and push vendors to deliver equivalent functionality so frontline clinicians do not lose capability during the transition.

items.title: Five years after Medicare coverage, AI diabetic eye screening reaches fewer than 1 in 1,500 Medicare beneficiaries with diabetes
items.summary: Four AI retinal screening systems are FDA-authorized and Medicare has paid for them since 2021, yet traditional Medicare claims rose only from about 400 in 2021 to 5,000 in 2024. Medicare's 2026 rates are $46.76 in an office and $60.27 in a hospital outpatient clinic, covering the image but not staff time, unreadable photos or follow-up. In five academic programs, 49% to 75% of photos were readable without dilation, and only 55% to 59% of positive screens in two programs reached an eye specialist. The proposed 2027 outpatient rule would create a payment category for these and similar software tools.
items.strategic_implication: AI adoption fails at the handoff, not the algorithm. Primary care and endocrinology leaders deploying autonomous screening should budget for imaging staff, dilation protocols and closed-loop referral tracking, and payers in value-based contracts should measure completed follow-up rather than screening volume.

items.title: Agentic AI benchmarks show best end-to-end healthcare task completion near 36% to 46%, as experts urge workflow-level evaluation
items.summary: In a MedCity commentary, John Snow Labs CTO David Talby argues that licensing-exam scores say little about safe clinical performance, citing a Nature study in which a frontier model scored 80% to 89% on public prompts but as low as 47% on unpublished ones. On PhysicianBench's 100 long-horizon tasks, the best model succeeded 46% of the time on first attempt, and on HealthAdminBench, which simulates an EHR, payer portals and fax, best end-to-end completion was 36.3%. Separately, Johns Hopkins professor Ritu Agarwal told Healthcare Dive the industry still has not moved from pilots to operational deployment and predicted consolidation toward large platform vendors.
items.strategic_implication: Vendor benchmark claims should not drive procurement. AI governance committees should require evidence on local data, end-to-end task completion and drift monitoring, set baseline metrics before go-live, and expect point-solution vendors to be absorbed by EHR and cloud platforms over the next few years.

editorial_buckets.name: Market and Industry Signals
editorial_buckets.synthesis: Optum is selling New York specialty practices to health systems, and Baylor Scott & White's plan is dropping most prior authorizations. Capital keeps concentrating in AI drug discovery, led by Isomorphic's $5 billion round and Flagship's London lab, while GLP-1 access splinters into employer defined-contribution models and a contested compounded market.

items.title: Optum sells New York physician practices to Northwell and Westchester Medical Center
items.summary: Regulatory filings show Optum is selling New York practice assets to two health systems. Northwell's Lenox Hill Hospital will take on up to 87 physicians and 47 advanced practice providers from Optum Medical Care (formerly CareMount), CareMount Health Solutions and ProHealth in OB/GYN, orthopedics, surgery, urology, allergy and hospital medicine, closing Dec. 7, along with a clinical collaboration agreement. Westchester Medical Center will acquire four Hudson Valley sites with 25 physicians, 11 advanced practice providers and 84 staff, including Crystal Run locations, closing Dec. 4. Optum said in June it was in talks to sell specialty services in the state.
items.strategic_implication: UnitedHealth is pruning specialty practices that do not fit its value-based primary care core, creating acquisition openings for health systems. Systems in markets with Optum, VillageMD or private-equity specialty groups should prepare to evaluate carve-outs, with attention to physician retention, payer contract assignment and FTC or state notice requirements.

items.title: Baylor Scott & White Health Plan to drop all in-network inpatient and more than 80% of outpatient prior authorizations Jan. 1
items.summary: Baylor Scott & White Health Plan will eliminate prior authorization for all in-network inpatient services and more than 80% of in-network outpatient requirements starting Jan. 1, across its commercial (fully insured and self-funded) and Medicare Advantage lines. The change applies to all in-network providers, including those outside the BSW system, and is expected to remove about 80% of in-network prior-authorization work. The plan will shift to "clinical stewardship," sharing data and reviewing utilization with its medical group. Its exits from Medicaid and individual markets were separate decisions.
items.strategic_implication: Provider-sponsored plans can move faster than national insurers on prior-auth relief, and BSW gives other integrated systems a template. Systems with their own plans should model the administrative savings against utilization risk, and all providers can cite the move in payer negotiations as evidence that gold-carding and data-sharing alternatives are workable.

items.title: Alphabet spinout Isomorphic Labs raises $5 billion, the largest biotech financing since 2022
items.summary: Isomorphic Labs closed a $5 billion Series C on Nov. 17 led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, with Alphabet, Andreessen Horowitz and others participating, six months after a $2.1 billion Series B. BioPharma Dive says the two rounds are the largest venture infusions this year among the firms it tracks. The company says it has positive preclinical oncology and immunology results and is preparing for clinical entry; partners include Novartis, Johnson & Johnson and Lilly. No AI-designed medicine has yet been approved.
items.strategic_implication: Capital is concentrating in a few AI drug-discovery platforms even as broader AI markets wobble. For health systems with research arms, the near-term opportunity is clinical trial partnerships as these companies enter human studies; for payers, AI-designed drugs remain years from formularies.

items.title: Flagship commits £100 million to a London lab for AI-native biotech companies, its first outside Cambridge, Mass.
items.summary: Flagship Pioneering launched Flagship Origination Lab, U.K., in London on Nov. 16 with an initial £100 million commitment, which it hopes to scale with an additional £500 million from partners. The lab will create AI-native platform companies in human and planetary health and expects to recruit about 50 scientist-entrepreneurs and operators.
items.strategic_implication: Company creation is globalizing, with the U.K. competing for AI-biotech talent and capital. U.S. academic medical centers that license research should note the competition for platform-company formation and keep their own tech-transfer and venture partnerships active.

items.title: Teladoc lets employers fund a fixed share of GLP-1 costs outside the pharmacy benefit
items.summary: Teladoc Health launched an option at HLTH for employers to contribute a fixed amount per employee per fill toward FDA-approved GLP-1s from Lilly and Novo Nordisk, outside traditional pharmacy benefits, with employees paying the balance. Employers can tie funding to engagement such as food tracking, weigh-ins and education, and Teladoc manages eligibility and clinical support. First clients launch Jan. 1; WTW data show about half of employers do not cover GLP-1s for weight loss.
items.strategic_implication: Defined-contribution GLP-1 coverage is emerging as a middle path between full coverage and exclusion, now that manufacturers sell direct at lower cash prices. Health systems that self-insure their workforce should compare this model with PBM coverage and their own weight-management programs, and payers should expect more carve-out pressure.

items.title: Telehealth leaders split at HLTH over compounded GLP-1s as FDA moves to restrict them
items.summary: Telehealth firms sell compounded GLP-1s for a few hundred dollars a month versus brand list prices above $1,000, even though FDA shortage-era compounding allowances ended in late 2024 and early 2025. Researchers estimate 27 million U.S. adults used a GLP-1 last year and at least 23% used compounded versions. FDA has logged nearly 1,000 adverse-event reports tied to compounded semaglutide and this spring proposed excluding semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide from ingredients large compounders may use. At HLTH, Sesame's CEO called the legal basis "tenuous," while OpenLoop said at least 6 million people could lose access if compounding stopped.
items.strategic_implication: A large share of GLP-1 use is happening outside traditional care and oversight. Health systems and payers should expect patients to transition from compounded products if FDA finalizes its exclusion, and can capture them with lower-cost branded direct-to-consumer options paired with clinical monitoring.

editorial_buckets.name: Provider Operations
editorial_buckets.synthesis: Leapfrog's fall grades reset safety benchmarks amid an unresolved methodology lawsuit, Cleveland Clinic is shifting revenue-cycle work upstream toward denials prevention and autonomous coding, and pediatric boarding of children in state custody remains a costly, largely invisible capacity drain.

items.title: Leapfrog fall 2026 grades: 900 'A' hospitals, three 'F's, and 450 hospitals ungraded for survey nonparticipation
items.summary: Leapfrog's fall 2026 Hospital Safety Grades, released Nov. 18, gave 900 hospitals an "A" and three an "F": Howard University Hospital, Roseland Community Hospital in Chicago and WVU Fairmont Medical Center, down from five "F"s in spring. Eleven hospitals have earned 30 consecutive "A"s since 2012. Connecticut led states at 64.3% "A" hospitals, Florida ranked ninth at 42.4%, and Iowa, the Dakotas, Vermont and Wyoming had none. For the second cycle, Leapfrog withheld grades from 450 hospitals that skipped its 2024 or 2025 survey, while its appeal of a ruling won by five Tenet Palm Beach hospitals is pending at the 11th Circuit.
items.strategic_implication: Grades still drive employer, consumer and board attention, but the methodology fight is unresolved. Quality leaders should benchmark against state peers, weigh the reputational cost of withheld grades against survey burden, and watch the 11th Circuit case, which could reshape how ratings organizations treat nonparticipating hospitals.

items.title: Cleveland Clinic targets denials prevention, upfront collections and autonomous inpatient coding in 2027 after $200 million revenue-cycle gain
items.summary: Cleveland Clinic expects more than $200 million in incremental revenue in 2026 and reports a 2.7% cost to collect across professional and hospital billing. For 2027, revenue cycle leaders are focused on predictive denial prevention, collecting patient cost shares before service through clearer estimates and MyChart payment options, stronger documentation and coding, and developing autonomous inpatient coding with a partner under governance controls. The system uses blinded payer scorecards and contract-rate audits, with litigation as a last resort, and calls patient balances its largest opportunity over the next two to three years.
items.strategic_implication: High performers are moving revenue-cycle work upstream and treating patient financial experience as the next margin lever. CFOs should benchmark cost to collect against 2.7%, set governance before deploying autonomous coding, and build payer scorecards to support denial escalations, much like AdventHealth's 2027 payer-grading plan.

items.title: Children in state custody are boarding in hospitals for months; Missouri spent $64.7 million over five years
items.summary: KFF Health News profiles a teen gun-violence survivor who spent more than 475 days across three stays at SSM Health Cardinal Glennon Children's Hospital, partly because no safe discharge option existed. Missouri spent more than $64.7 million boarding children in state custody in hospitals over five years, which the state hospital association calls an undercount, and recorded 648 boarded youths in the fiscal year ending in June. Illinois reported 304 youths in psychiatric hospitals beyond medical necessity and 312 waiting more than 24 hours in emergency departments in fiscal 2025.
items.strategic_implication: Social stays block beds and generate uncompensated cost that rarely shows up in throughput dashboards. Children's hospitals and pediatric units should track boarding days separately, document them for state reimbursement, and press child-welfare and Medicaid agencies for step-down placements and enhanced foster-care rates.

editorial_buckets.name: Workforce & Clinical Practice
editorial_buckets.synthesis: Proposals to unbundle medical school reflect pressure to shorten physician training, and the 2025 preterm birth rate of 10.4% shows maternal and infant outcomes are still well short of national targets.

items.title: STAT series proposes unbundling medical school with a centralized digital pre-clerkship curriculum
items.summary: In the second essay of a STAT First Opinion series on redesigning medical school, M.D./Ph.D. student Alex Serafini proposes a centralized digital "core-to-clinic" curriculum for pre-clerkship studies, open to students who meet baseline criteria such as a minimum MCAT score, before hands-on training at clinical sites. He asks why hundreds of schools independently build parallel versions of the same curriculum. The first essay argued medical school should begin after Step 1.
items.strategic_implication: Pressure to shorten and cheapen physician training is growing alongside workforce shortages. Health systems with teaching programs should watch for accelerated and decentralized pathways that could expand clinical-site training roles, and consider how such models might feed rural and primary care pipelines.

items.title: U.S. preterm birth rate was 10.4% in 2025, a full point above the Healthy People 2030 target
items.summary: STAT's Morning Rounds reports the 2025 U.S. preterm birth rate was 10.4%, compared with the Healthy People 2030 target of 9.4%; only nine states met the target. Sixteen states met the infant mortality goal of five deaths per 1,000 births, and the rate for Black infants remained twice the national average.
items.strategic_implication: Maternal and infant outcomes remain a persistent quality and equity gap, particularly as Medicaid coverage changes take effect. Obstetric service lines and Medicaid plans should prioritize prenatal access, postpartum coverage continuity and rural labor-and-delivery capacity, where closures continue to widen gaps.

editions.headline: Today's Healthcare Insights
editions.subheadline: A cross-source executive briefing on healthcare policy, operations, and market signals.
editions.summary_note: CMS proposed its CRUSH anti-fraud rule, projecting $90 billion in 10-year savings mostly from Medicare Advantage audits, and a Lown analysis found 52% of nonprofit hospitals get more in tax breaks than they return. CVS put a roughly $350-a-month break-even price on GLP-1s, health AI spending doubled to $3.7 billion, AdventHealth will start grading payers in 2027, and J&J agreed to buy Ollin for $2.2 billion. Sources include STAT, KFF Health News, Healthcare Dive, BioPharma Dive, MedCity News and Becker's.

Checked against the prior 30 editions for repeats; excluded the Medicaid work-requirement delay and hospital preparation follow-ups, the Summit ivonescimab rejection, CG Oncology's bladder cancer data and Apple-OpenEvidence (all covered Nov. 16), PHI's lawsuits against employers (covered Nov. 11) and Oura's Counsel Health deal (covered Nov. 11). The American Healthcare Systems item is a new Illinois development after the Nov. 12 Florida settlement item. Screened but not itemized: STAT's biotech-rebound column (paywalled), executive appointments at Cook Children's and a Massachusetts hospital, a HLTH primary-care AI panel, a KFF consumer explainer on moving states, INVEST conference startup coverage and opinion pieces.

editorial_buckets.name: Policy, Payment, and Regulation
editorial_buckets.synthesis: CMS's CRUSH proposal turns program integrity into a $90 billion Medicare Advantage audit agenda while tightening provider enrollment and Medicaid overpayment rules, with comments due Jan. 19. A new Lown analysis renews pressure on nonprofit tax exemptions, FDA opened a supplement pathway for the drug NAC, NIAID's new permanent director confirms a shift away from pandemic preparedness, and federal addiction policy is tilting toward faith-based recovery even as harm-reduction funding shrinks.

items.title: CMS proposes CRUSH anti-fraud rule projecting $90 billion in 10-year savings, mostly from Medicare Advantage audits
items.summary: CMS on Nov. 16 proposed the Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare (CRUSH) rule spanning Medicare, Medicaid/CHIP and the ACA marketplace, with comments due Jan. 19, 2027. CMS projects nearly $90 billion in federal savings over 10 years; STAT reports agency officials said all of it comes from more aggressive Medicare Advantage risk-adjustment audits, which could extrapolate back to 2018 at roughly $9 billion per payment year. Provider-facing changes include a 30-day window (down from 90) to report enrollment changes, traditional-Medicare screening for clinicians billing MA plans two years after finalization, a 60-day rule to report and return Medicaid fee-for-service overpayments, and penalties for states with eligibility error rates above 3%.
items.strategic_implication: MA plans face the largest financial exposure, and that pressure will likely flow to providers through tighter documentation demands and coding scrutiny. Hospitals and medical groups should audit enrollment-change reporting processes now for the 30-day standard, confirm every MA-billing clinician is enrolled in traditional Medicare, and weigh filing comments before Jan. 19.

items.title: Lown Institute: 52% of nonprofit hospitals received more in tax breaks than they returned in charity care and community investment
items.summary: A Lown Institute analysis released Nov. 17 of 3,037 nonprofit hospitals using FY2023 data found 52% ran a 'fair share' deficit, receiving $27.5 billion in tax exemptions while spending $12 billion on financial assistance, subsidized services and community investment, a $15.5 billion gap. Hospitals in surplus provided $13.8 billion more than their exemptions were worth. California, Florida, Illinois and Ohio each had deficits above $1 billion, and the method excludes Medicaid shortfalls, education and research, which hospitals typically count as community benefit.
items.strategic_implication: Annual fair-share rankings feed state and federal scrutiny of tax exemptions, particularly in Florida and other large-deficit states. Nonprofit boards should know how their Form 990 figures look under Lown's narrower definition and be ready to explain the gap between reported community benefit and charity care.

items.title: FDA proposes new regulatory category that lets the drug NAC be sold as a dietary supplement
items.summary: FDA on Nov. 16 proposed classifying N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC), approved as a drug since 1963 and as an acetaminophen-overdose treatment since 1985, as the agency's first 'Dietary Ingredient Not Excluded from the Dietary Supplement Definition.' FDA rules generally bar approved drugs from the supplement category; the proposal resolves a long legal gray area over NAC sold over the counter. STAT describes it as a win for supplement proponents, including the MAHA movement; full details are behind STAT's paywall.
items.strategic_implication: The new category creates a template that could be applied to other drug-derived ingredients, loosening the drug-supplement boundary. Pharmacy, clinical and patient-safety leaders should watch whether further ingredients follow and reinforce supplement-use screening during medication reconciliation.

items.title: Acting NIAID head John Powers III named permanent director, with a mandate to shift focus beyond HIV and pandemic preparedness
items.summary: NIH named John Powers III, a physician-scientist who has led NIAID in an acting capacity since June, as the institute's permanent director, STAT reported Nov. 16-17. Powers co-authored a paper with NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya arguing NIAID should shift its emphasis from HIV and pandemic preparedness toward broader infectious disease and immunology. His predecessor, Jeanne Marrazzo, was forced out in 2025 after objecting to grant terminations.
items.strategic_implication: Permanent leadership locks in a reprioritized NIAID portfolio. Academic medical centers and health-security programs dependent on HIV, emerging-pathogen and preparedness grants should plan for continued funding pressure and look for alignment with the institute's broader infectious-disease and immunology framing.

items.title: HHS steers more federal support toward faith-based addiction recovery as experts warn of gaps in evidence-based care
items.summary: STAT reported Nov. 17 that the administration's 2026 National Drug Control Strategy and Great American Recovery Initiative promote faith-based recovery, and HHS has awarded $500,000 each to Alabama, Kansas and West Virginia for faith-based prevention. SAMHSA grant terms now caution against medication-only treatment. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. recently visited Iowa's Sheepgate, whose yearlong programs prohibit methadone and allow Suboxone only if tapered within three months; addiction experts urged funding safeguards that require evidence-based care.
items.strategic_implication: Health systems that refer patients to community recovery partners should verify partners' policies on medications for opioid use disorder, since a referral to a program that bars methadone can disrupt treatment. Expect future SAMHSA notices to favor faith-based applicants and plan partnerships accordingly.

items.title: SAMHSA ban on funding drug test strips leaves local harm-reduction groups unable to track tainted supply
items.summary: KFF Health News reported Nov. 17 that SAMHSA said in April its funds could no longer buy test strips for fentanyl, xylazine, medetomidine or other substances, part of a more than $300 million national reduction in overdose-prevention and treatment funding. In North Carolina, SAMHSA had been the state opioid response program's only source of fentanyl and xylazine strips; small volunteer groups are now paying out of pocket. UNC-Chapel Hill's street drug lab has detected about 500 unique substances since 2022.
items.strategic_implication: Less community drug checking means emergency departments may be the first to detect new adulterants such as medetomidine. Hospitals should strengthen links with local drug-checking labs and health departments and update ED protocols for atypical overdose and withdrawal presentations.

editorial_buckets.name: Digital Health and AI
editorial_buckets.synthesis: HLTH-week data show AI spending doubled to $3.7 billion, with ambient scribing consolidating around Microsoft and Epic and new money moving to clinical copilots and front-office tools. Still, only 30% of organizations have scaled advanced AI, held back by integration and cost. Kaiser's physician group launched a spinout vehicle, and Noom brought a wearable to employer obesity programs.

items.title: Health AI spending more than doubles to $3.7 billion as providers shift money to clinical copilots and front-office AI
items.summary: A Menlo Partners report surveying more than 550 healthcare and life sciences executives found healthcare AI spending reached $3.7 billion, more than double the prior year, with providers accounting for 77%, Healthcare Dive reported Nov. 16. Provider spending on clinical copilots and patient engagement/front-office tools grew about fivefold, to $550 million and $450 million, while ambient scribing and coding spend grew less than twofold. Microsoft Dragon Copilot and Epic Art captured 68% of new ambient-scribing dollars in 2026, and startups lost 13 points of share.
items.strategic_implication: Ambient scribing is consolidating around EHR-native vendors, so the competitive frontier has moved to clinical decision support and patient access. Systems should rationalize point-solution scribe contracts against EHR-bundled options and direct new budget to front-office and copilot use cases with measurable access or throughput gains.

items.title: Google survey: only 30% of healthcare organizations have scaled advanced or agentic AI, trailing other industries
items.summary: A Google Cloud survey of more than 250 healthcare executives found nearly 60% struggle with integration and deployment when moving AI from pilot to production, and 40% have paused initiatives over unpredictable costs, Healthcare Dive reported Nov. 16. Only 30% said they had scaled advanced or agentic AI across operations, 13 points below the all-industry benchmark, and more than 80% cited cost as a barrier to reducing dependence on existing AI vendors.
items.strategic_implication: The binding constraint on AI value is operational, not technical: integration capacity, cost predictability and vendor lock-in. Leaders should require usage-based cost models and exit terms in AI contracts and fund integration staff alongside pilots rather than after them.

items.title: The Permanente Medical Group launches Permanentech to commercialize clinician-built tools, starting with infusion no-show AI
items.summary: The Permanente Medical Group, Kaiser Permanente's roughly 10,000-physician Northern California group, launched Permanentech at HLTH on Nov. 16 to turn frontline clinician ideas into products, partnerships and spinout companies. Its first portfolio company, Wrapt Health, uses AI to predict missed infusion appointments, automate outreach and prioritize cases; it operates across 22 sites and 524 infusion chairs and reports reduced no-show rates.
items.strategic_implication: Large physician groups are treating operational know-how as a commercial asset. Health systems with strong clinical informatics talent can consider similar venture structures, and infusion-center leaders should evaluate predictive scheduling, since unused chairs and wasted drug represent direct margin.

items.title: Noom unveils wearable for employer and health-plan obesity programs, citing early gains among GLP-1 users
items.summary: Noom announced the Noom Band at HLTH, a Sensor Bio-powered wearable tracking activity, sleep, heart rate, HRV and oxygen saturation, launching in early 2027 for all employer and health-plan clients at no added upfront cost, MedCity News reported Nov. 16. Noom said GLP-1 users with a connected wearable were 34% more likely to lose 20 pounds by month four; CEO Geoff Cook said the results are preliminary and not peer-reviewed.
items.strategic_implication: Obesity-program vendors are bundling devices and behavior support to justify their place beside costly GLP-1 coverage. Employers and plans should request outcomes and adherence data, not engagement metrics, before expanding these programs.

editorial_buckets.name: Market and Industry Signals
editorial_buckets.synthesis: CVS set a roughly $350-a-month break-even price for GLP-1s, giving employers a benchmark for 2027 negotiations. Medicare Advantage enrollment is concentrating in Humana and UnitedHealthcare as 4.3 million beneficiaries face plan terminations. On the biopharma side, J&J's $2.2 billion Ollin deal, Roche's giredestrant approval, Marrow's $173 million launch and Sellas' AML result signal continued deal and oncology momentum, while tobacco companies test new oral nicotine formats.

items.title: CVS says GLP-1s become cost-saving for payers at about $350 a month, pressing Lilly and Novo on price
items.summary: A CVS Health white paper released at HLTH, based on three years of Aetna commercial claims, found continuing GLP-1 users had 34% to 42% fewer hospitalizations and a 14% lower likelihood of major cardiovascular events, Healthcare Dive reported Nov. 16. Plan sponsors saved $9,400 per person in medical costs but spent $13,300 more on prescriptions, a $3,900 net cost. CVS said prices of roughly $350 a month or less would make the drugs cost-saving; employers typically pay $617 to $766 monthly, versus $245 in Medicare's pilot.
items.strategic_implication: A large PBM-insurer has put a concrete break-even price in front of employers, which strengthens purchaser leverage in 2027 negotiations. Benefit consultants and self-insured health systems should model coverage decisions against the $350 benchmark and use outcomes data, not list price alone, to set utilization criteria.

items.title: Humana and UnitedHealthcare capture 58% of early Medicare Advantage enrollment applications as plan terminations climb
items.summary: A Spark Advisors analysis of applications from Oct. 15 to Nov. 6 found Humana with 30% and UnitedHealthcare with 28% of Medicare Advantage enrollments, with UnitedHealthcare volume up 49% year over year and Humana's down 11%, Becker's reported. About 4.3 million beneficiaries' MA plans or Part D plans will terminate Dec. 31, compared with 2.9 million a year earlier; 46.4% of beneficiaries face higher out-of-pocket maximums, and Devoted Health took 18% of switchers.
items.strategic_implication: Plan exits and benefit cuts will shuffle payer mix on Jan. 1. Revenue-cycle and access teams should map which local plans are terminating, prepare to re-verify coverage for high volumes of switching patients in January and build authorization relationships with gaining plans such as Devoted.

items.title: J&J agrees to buy Ollin Biosciences for $2.2 billion upfront, with Blackstone funding $750 million of Phase 3 eye-drug trials
items.summary: Johnson & Johnson agreed Nov. 16 to acquire Ollin Biosciences for $2.2 billion upfront plus up to $1.1 billion in milestones, gaining OLN324, a VEGF/Ang2 drug in Phase 3 testing for wet AMD and diabetic macular edema that could compete with Roche's Vabysmo and Regeneron's Eylea. Blackstone Life Sciences will provide $750 million to fund the late-stage trials, and the drug originated at Shanghai-based Innovent Biologics.
items.strategic_implication: Big pharma is increasingly pairing China-sourced assets with private-capital trial financing to share late-stage risk. For retina practices and health-system pharmacy, more long-acting entrants could intensify competition and pricing in one of Medicare Part B's highest-spend drug classes later this decade.

items.title: FDA approves Roche's oral SERD giredestrant for ESR1-mutated advanced breast cancer
items.summary: FDA on Nov. 16 approved Roche's Wilserdly (giredestrant), an oral selective estrogen receptor degrader, for HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer with an ESR1 mutation, based on the evERA trial showing longer time to progression, STAT reported. Roche has said the drug could become its top-selling product ever, though estimates vary; the full article is paywalled.
items.strategic_implication: Approval adds to the ESR1-mutation-directed options, making routine ESR1 testing at progression more important. Oncology service lines should confirm liquid-biopsy testing workflows and prepare for specialty-pharmacy and prior-authorization demands as oral options expand.

items.title: Marrow Therapeutics launches with $173 million to develop a redosable injectable alternative to sickle cell gene therapy
items.summary: Marrow Therapeutics emerged from stealth Nov. 17 with $173 million in Series A and B financing from 11 investors, including Scion Life Sciences, OrbiMed and venBio. Its lead drug, MAR-101, is an antibody-siRNA conjugate meant to reactivate fetal hemoglobin and could be dosed repeatedly by injection for sickle cell disease and beta thalassemia; trial timing has not been disclosed. Approved gene therapies Casgevy and Lyfgenia require cell collection, chemotherapy conditioning and specialized centers.
items.strategic_implication: Investors are betting that the infrastructure burden of curative gene therapy leaves room for simpler, outpatient-deliverable options. Sickle cell programs should keep building comprehensive care capacity, since any such therapy is years away and current gene-therapy uptake stays constrained by center capacity.

items.title: Sellas says its AML immunotherapy cut the risk of death by 41% in a Phase 3 trial
items.summary: Sellas Life Sciences said Nov. 17 that galinpepimut-S reduced the risk of death by 41% compared with standard treatment in patients with advanced-stage acute myeloid leukemia, meeting the Phase 3 trial's main goal, STAT reported. STAT called the result unexpected; its biotech columnist had predicted in September that the drug would fail. Full trial data were not available in the visible text.
items.strategic_implication: The topline survival result is company-reported and needs full data and peer review before it changes practice. Hematologic oncology programs should track the results for possible FDA filing and maintenance-therapy pathways in AML.

items.title: Capsida reports progress on screening for the safety risk behind a fatal brain gene therapy trial case
items.summary: Capsida Biotherapeutics researchers presented findings on the death of a patient in its brain-disease gene therapy trial last year; STAT's Morning Rounds noted a 3-year-old died of brain swelling 65 hours after treatment. Researchers did not pinpoint the cause but proposed experiments, including tests in monkeys, to screen future therapies, STAT reported Nov. 17; the full report is paywalled.
items.strategic_implication: Safety screening for CNS-targeted gene therapies is still developing, which will shape regulatory expectations and trial pace. Academic centers hosting such trials should reinforce informed-consent language and acute neurological monitoring protocols.

items.title: Tobacco firms test flavored dissolving nicotine tablets abroad as U.S. child nicotine poisonings rise
items.summary: Philip Morris International has introduced mint Zyn Melts in the U.K. and Switzerland, and Japan Tobacco International launched Perlz in the U.K. in May, STAT and The Examination reported Nov. 17. Global nicotine-pouch sales reached $9.2 billion in 2025, with volume forecast to grow 20.5% a year. U.S. nicotine-poisoning calls nearly doubled from 2024 to 2025, with three-quarters of 2025 cases involving children under 6.
items.strategic_implication: Candy-like nicotine formats raise youth-initiation and pediatric-ingestion risks before U.S. regulators act on them. Pediatric practices, poison-control partners and school-health programs should add newer oral nicotine products to screening and anticipatory guidance.

editorial_buckets.name: Provider Operations
editorial_buckets.synthesis: AdventHealth is formalizing payer scorecards and building litigation capacity, showing how large systems are pushing back on denial friction. American Healthcare Systems' Illinois hospital shows the knock-on effects of operator distress on EMS and trauma coverage, and Ascension Wisconsin's $340 million plan targets deferred imaging, equipment and behavioral health capacity.

items.title: AdventHealth will begin grading payers on scorecards in 2027 and is staffing up for arbitration and litigation
items.summary: AdventHealth plans to start rating payers in 2027 on administrative friction, cost of doing business, time to pay and turnaround on records requests and appeals, reviewing the scorecards at quarterly payer meetings, revenue cycle SVP Tim Reiner told Becker's. About 10% to 12% of AdventHealth's claims are initially denied and 1.5% to 3% are ultimately written off, with prior authorization tied to about a quarter of denials. The Florida system is hiring paralegals and attorneys to use arbitration and litigation more often.
items.strategic_implication: Large systems are formalizing payer performance management and becoming more willing to litigate. Florida providers in AdventHealth markets should expect contract talks to sharpen, and any revenue-cycle leader can adopt a similar scorecard to quantify the cost of payer friction ahead of renegotiations.

items.title: American Healthcare Systems' Waukegan hospital leans on medical staff leaders amid diversion, low census and payroll strain
items.summary: Vista Medical Center East in Waukegan, Ill., owned by American Healthcare Systems, went on ambulance bypass in early November amid payroll struggles and said Nov. 16 it had a low census and is giving medical executive committee members a bigger leadership role, Becker's reported. Illinois revoked its Level 2 trauma designation in late October after its anesthesia group suspended services over missed payments. The update follows CEO Mike Sarian's early-November settlement of Florida lawsuits, which relinquished control of five Florida facilities.
items.strategic_implication: This shows how a distressed hospital operator's problems spread across markets, affecting trauma coverage and EMS routing. Neighboring systems and county EMS agencies in AHS markets should plan for sustained diversion surges, and boards should treat physician-led interim governance as a warning sign of instability.

items.title: Ascension Wisconsin commits $340 million to multi-year facility, equipment and behavioral-health upgrades
items.summary: Ascension Wisconsin announced Nov. 16 a $340 million multi-year infrastructure plan, funded with $315 million from Ascension and $25 million from its foundation. The plan replaces 16 MRI, 20 CT and 13 X-ray machines and more than 560 beds, budgets $31 million for physiologic monitoring and includes a $10 million inpatient behavioral health expansion at St. Francis Hospital in Milwaukee to 61 beds.
items.strategic_implication: After years of portfolio trimming, Ascension is reinvesting in markets it kept, with an emphasis on deferred imaging and monitoring replacement. Competing systems in southeastern Wisconsin should expect stronger imaging and behavioral health positioning, and other systems can use the mix as a benchmark for catching up on deferred capital.

editorial_buckets.name: Workforce & Clinical Practice
editorial_buckets.synthesis: A final court ruling keeps visa terms for international researchers open-ended for now, protecting academic research staffing. Early daraxonrasib use shows that access to new oral cancer drugs depends on prior-authorization speed and nurse-led toxicity management.

items.title: Federal judge issues final ruling striking down four-year visa cap for international graduate students and postdocs
items.summary: U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV in Boston on Nov. 16 issued a final ruling striking down the administration's rule capping 'duration of status' visas at four years, calling it 'arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion,' STAT reported. Universities and research advocates had warned the cap would deter international students, since graduate degrees often run longer than four years. The government's appeal of Saylor's earlier temporary block remains pending.
items.strategic_implication: The ruling preserves, for now, an international pipeline that academic medical centers depend on for research labs and future physician-scientists. Research leaders should still plan for an appeal and continued immigration-policy volatility in postdoc recruiting.

items.title: Cancer centers report one-to-two-week starts on daraxonrasib for pancreatic cancer, with insurance approval the main bottleneck
items.summary: Nearly three months after FDA approved daraxonrasib for metastatic pancreatic cancer on Aug. 26, leaders at seven organizations, including Penn Medicine, Sylvester, UC San Diego Health and UW Health, told Becker's patients are often starting within one to two weeks, though Lowell General reported three to four weeks. Insurance approval is the main bottleneck. Jefferson estimates at least a third of patients need dose reductions for rash, mouth sores or diarrhea, and resistance develops after roughly seven months in nearly all patients.
items.strategic_implication: Getting a breakthrough oral oncolytic to patients depends on fast authorization and toxicity management. Oncology programs should give specialty-pharmacy navigators clear ownership of prior authorization and set nurse-led side-effect protocols, which matters especially for community sites.

editions.subheadline: A cross-source executive briefing on healthcare policy, operations, and market signals.
editions.summary_note: The administration delayed Medicaid work-requirement enforcement six months to July 1, 2027, and PAHO concluded the U.S. has lost measles elimination status. CommonSpirit posted a $544 million quarterly operating loss, Mayo Clinic named its AI leader as CEO, FDA rejected Summit's lung cancer drug ivonescimab, and Sen. Cassidy plans a No Surprises Act reform bill. Sources include STAT, KFF Health News, Healthcare Dive, BioPharma Dive, MedCity News and Becker's.
